query:
We make small batches of aluminium-alloy powder by ultrasonic atomization (AMAZEMET rePOWDER, induction-heated module). We are deciding how to turn **pure aluminium powder** (gas-atomized, roughly 15-63 µm, alone or blended with alloying-element or master-alloy powders) into **green parts** that we then melt in the atomizer crucible together with solid alloy (6063 rod, 4047). We want a **pros-and-cons comparison of two consolidation routes**, (A) powder-metallurgy pressing under vacuum and (B) cold isostatic pressing (CIP), judged on **safety** first, then simplicity, speed, cost, and whether the green part will melt, coalesce and mix into the rest of the melt. Please answer from the literature, with citations (DOIs where possible), give numbers wherever the sources have them, and say explicitly which conclusions come from direct evidence for aluminium and which are extrapolated from other metals or from general PM practice.

**Set-up.** Graphite crucible (BN-coated), induction heated, 10-11 cm deep, with a sealing (stopper) rod down the middle; the melt is bottom-poured through a ~0.7 mm hBN nozzle onto a 40 kHz vibrating molybdenum plate. The charge is loaded cold. The chamber is then evacuated and back-filled with argon several times ("gas washes"), including while the charge is held at about 500 °C and still solid. It is then melted under argon at about 0.2 bar overpressure (13-20 ppm O2), set point 810-840 °C, held about 2 minutes (we may extend this to 5-10 minutes), with no mechanical stirring beyond the induction field. Charges are 170-350 g. Every piece must be under 20 mm across to fit between the stopper rod and the crucible wall, so a green part would be a slug about 19 mm in diameter and 20-60 mm long (roughly 10-40 g).

**What we already know** (our own runs, and an earlier literature review on 2026-11-02 that you do not need to repeat). Loose gas-atomized powder sealed in a 6063 cup did not consolidate in one run (AlSi10Mg) and did in another (4047); the oxide shell on each particle, plus MgO or spinel when Mg is present, keeps the molten droplets apart. Cold uniaxial pressing of Al powder reaches about 85 % relative density at about 100 MPa and 92-98 % at 250-580 MPa; it cracks the oxide but does not remove it. Pores start to close above roughly 85-90 % density, so a denser compact can seal in air, adsorbed water and water from hydrated oxide. The equipment maker warned that powder compressed inside a closed aluminium cup could eject molten metal, presumably from trapped gas. Die lubricants add gas and carbon. Cast master alloys, or an arc-melted button made from the weighed powders, were ranked above any pressed compact.

**The two routes to compare.**
- **(A) "Powder metallurgy under vacuum":** uniaxial die pressing with the die cavity evacuated before and during pressing (an evacuable die with a vacuum port and O-ring seals, or a die inside a vacuum chamber or glovebox), with or without vacuum drying or degassing of the loose powder beforehand. Please also cover the natural extensions: pressing followed by vacuum sintering or degassing, and vacuum hot pressing (for example 300-550 °C).
- **(B) Cold isostatic pressing (CIP):** powder filled into a flexible elastomer mould (polyurethane, latex, silicone or rubber bag), optionally evacuated and sealed, and pressed hydrostatically (typically 100-400 MPa) by a water-based fluid or oil. Wet-bag versus dry-bag; buying a small laboratory CIP versus sending parts to a toll-pressing service. Also the combination of A and B: powder vacuum-degassed first, sealed in an evacuated bag, then cold isostatically pressed.

**Please address:**

1. **Pros and cons of each route (and its sub-variants) for pure aluminium powder**, ideally as a table covering: process safety; safety of the green part when melted in our crucible; green density achievable versus pressure, and its uniformity (density gradients and low-density zones in uniaxially pressed slugs with height-to-diameter ratios of about 1-3, versus isostatic pressing); green strength, edge integrity and powder shedding during handling; the need for lubricants and their effect; contamination (lubricant residue, bag material, pressing fluid, die wear); dimensional control (our 20 mm limit, CIP shrinkage and shape tolerance); oxide-film disruption (does hydrostatic loading in CIP break the particle oxide films more or less than the shear in a uniaxial die?); residual gas and moisture in the part; simplicity and the skill needed; time per part and per batch; and cost (equipment capital, tooling and consumables, and toll-service pricing if published).
2. **Which route makes the safer green part to melt in the atomizer, and why.** Quantify where possible: adsorbed and chemically bound water on gas-atomized Al powder (mass %, or mL H2 per 100 g Al) and the temperatures at which it is released; the open-to-closed porosity transition for Al compacts; how much evacuating the die or the CIP bag before pressing reduces the trapped gas; and whether an open-pore green compact heated slowly through our vacuum and argon washes up to about 500 °C would degas in place before its pores close. What are the failure modes: a CIP bag leak or puncture that lets water or oil into the powder (and the hydrogen that water generates with freshly exposed Al), lubricant decomposition, trapped air expanding on heating, lamination or end-capping cracks from uniaxial pressing?
3. **Process hazards of each route** when handling fine pure Al powder: combustible-dust and ignition risks while filling dies or bags, drawing fine powder into a vacuum line or pump, venting an evacuated die to air, contact with the CIP fluid, stored energy in the high-pressure vessel, and safe practice for each (inert handling, filters, grounding, PPE).
4. **Melt-in and mixing feasibility.** Would a green part from either route (at what density) melt, coalesce and mix into a 6063 melt at 810-840 °C under argon within 2-10 minutes with only induction stirring? Does CIP versus uniaxial pressing versus vacuum hot pressing change coalescence, metal yield, dross or oxide inclusions on remelting? Use evidence from remelting Al powder compacts, chip or swarf briquettes, PM parts and foundry alloying tablets. If alloying powders (Si, Cu, Mg, Mn, Fe, Ni, Ti, Zr) are blended into the pure Al before pressing: segregation while filling, and exothermic reactions between Al and these powders on heating (for example the self-propagating Al-Ni, Al-Ti, Al-Fe or Al-Zr reactions in pressed compacts, and how compact density affects ignition), and whether these help or hurt safety and dissolution.
5. **A practical recipe for each route** for a 19 mm diameter by 20-60 mm slug: pressure, dwell, evacuation level, drying or degassing temperature and time, lubricant (or none), mould or die material and sizing, expected density, and how to check a part before it goes into the crucible (Archimedes density and open porosity, a weight-loss or gas-release test on heating). What press force, or what CIP vessel size and pressure rating, does this need?
6. **Recommendation:** which route, or neither, would you choose for a university lab making a few such parts per week, and when would each be the wrong choice? Compare briefly with buying cast master alloys or arc-melting a button from the weighed powders.
task_summary: Compare Vacuum Uniaxial Powder Metallurgy Versus Cold Isostatic Pressing For Aluminium Green Parts

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions

        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions

        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions

    DesignAllocation:

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.

Use the tools to answer the question: We make small batches of aluminium-alloy powder by ultrasonic atomization (AMAZEMET rePOWDER, induction-heated module). We are deciding how to turn **pure aluminium powder** (gas-atomized, roughly 15-63 µm, alone or blended with alloying-element or master-alloy powders) into **green parts** that we then melt in the atomizer crucible together with solid alloy (6063 rod, 4047). We want a **pros-and-cons comparison of two consolidation routes**, (A) powder-metallurgy pressing under vacuum and (B) cold isostatic pressing (CIP), judged on **safety** first, then simplicity, speed, cost, and whether the green part will melt, coalesce and mix into the rest of the melt. Please answer from the literature, with citations (DOIs where possible), give numbers wherever the sources have them, and say explicitly which conclusions come from direct evidence for aluminium and which are extrapolated from other metals or from general PM practice.

**Set-up.** Graphite crucible (BN-coated), induction heated, 10-11 cm deep, with a sealing (stopper) rod down the middle; the melt is bottom-poured through a ~0.7 mm hBN nozzle onto a 40 kHz vibrating molybdenum plate. The charge is loaded cold. The chamber is then evacuated and back-filled with argon several times ("gas washes"), including while the charge is held at about 500 °C and still solid. It is then melted under argon at about 0.2 bar overpressure (13-20 ppm O2), set point 810-840 °C, held about 2 minutes (we may extend this to 5-10 minutes), with no mechanical stirring beyond the induction field. Charges are 170-350 g. Every piece must be under 20 mm across to fit between the stopper rod and the crucible wall, so a green part would be a slug about 19 mm in diameter and 20-60 mm long (roughly 10-40 g).

**What we already know** (our own runs, and an earlier literature review on 2026-11-02 that you do not need to repeat). Loose gas-atomized powder sealed in a 6063 cup did not consolidate in one run (AlSi10Mg) and did in another (4047); the oxide shell on each particle, plus MgO or spinel when Mg is present, keeps the molten droplets apart. Cold uniaxial pressing of Al powder reaches about 85 % relative density at about 100 MPa and 92-98 % at 250-580 MPa; it cracks the oxide but does not remove it. Pores start to close above roughly 85-90 % density, so a denser compact can seal in air, adsorbed water and water from hydrated oxide. The equipment maker warned that powder compressed inside a closed aluminium cup could eject molten metal, presumably from trapped gas. Die lubricants add gas and carbon. Cast master alloys, or an arc-melted button made from the weighed powders, were ranked above any pressed compact.

**The two routes to compare.**
- **(A) "Powder metallurgy under vacuum":** uniaxial die pressing with the die cavity evacuated before and during pressing (an evacuable die with a vacuum port and O-ring seals, or a die inside a vacuum chamber or glovebox), with or without vacuum drying or degassing of the loose powder beforehand. Please also cover the natural extensions: pressing followed by vacuum sintering or degassing, and vacuum hot pressing (for example 300-550 °C).
- **(B) Cold isostatic pressing (CIP):** powder filled into a flexible elastomer mould (polyurethane, latex, silicone or rubber bag), optionally evacuated and sealed, and pressed hydrostatically (typically 100-400 MPa) by a water-based fluid or oil. Wet-bag versus dry-bag; buying a small laboratory CIP versus sending parts to a toll-pressing service. Also the combination of A and B: powder vacuum-degassed first, sealed in an evacuated bag, then cold isostatically pressed.

**Please address:**

1. **Pros and cons of each route (and its sub-variants) for pure aluminium powder**, ideally as a table covering: process safety; safety of the green part when melted in our crucible; green density achievable versus pressure, and its uniformity (density gradients and low-density zones in uniaxially pressed slugs with height-to-diameter ratios of about 1-3, versus isostatic pressing); green strength, edge integrity and powder shedding during handling; the need for lubricants and their effect; contamination (lubricant residue, bag material, pressing fluid, die wear); dimensional control (our 20 mm limit, CIP shrinkage and shape tolerance); oxide-film disruption (does hydrostatic loading in CIP break the particle oxide films more or less than the shear in a uniaxial die?); residual gas and moisture in the part; simplicity and the skill needed; time per part and per batch; and cost (equipment capital, tooling and consumables, and toll-service pricing if published).
2. **Which route makes the safer green part to melt in the atomizer, and why.** Quantify where possible: adsorbed and chemically bound water on gas-atomized Al powder (mass %, or mL H2 per 100 g Al) and the temperatures at which it is released; the open-to-closed porosity transition for Al compacts; how much evacuating the die or the CIP bag before pressing reduces the trapped gas; and whether an open-pore green compact heated slowly through our vacuum and argon washes up to about 500 °C would degas in place before its pores close. What are the failure modes: a CIP bag leak or puncture that lets water or oil into the powder (and the hydrogen that water generates with freshly exposed Al), lubricant decomposition, trapped air expanding on heating, lamination or end-capping cracks from uniaxial pressing?
3. **Process hazards of each route** when handling fine pure Al powder: combustible-dust and ignition risks while filling dies or bags, drawing fine powder into a vacuum line or pump, venting an evacuated die to air, contact with the CIP fluid, stored energy in the high-pressure vessel, and safe practice for each (inert handling, filters, grounding, PPE).
4. **Melt-in and mixing feasibility.** Would a green part from either route (at what density) melt, coalesce and mix into a 6063 melt at 810-840 °C under argon within 2-10 minutes with only induction stirring? Does CIP versus uniaxial pressing versus vacuum hot pressing change coalescence, metal yield, dross or oxide inclusions on remelting? Use evidence from remelting Al powder compacts, chip or swarf briquettes, PM parts and foundry alloying tablets. If alloying powders (Si, Cu, Mg, Mn, Fe, Ni, Ti, Zr) are blended into the pure Al before pressing: segregation while filling, and exothermic reactions between Al and these powders on heating (for example the self-propagating Al-Ni, Al-Ti, Al-Fe or Al-Zr reactions in pressed compacts, and how compact density affects ignition), and whether these help or hurt safety and dissolution.
5. **A practical recipe for each route** for a 19 mm diameter by 20-60 mm slug: pressure, dwell, evacuation level, drying or degassing temperature and time, lubricant (or none), mould or die material and sizing, expected density, and how to check a part before it goes into the crucible (Archimedes density and open porosity, a weight-loss or gas-release test on heating). What press force, or what CIP vessel size and pressure rating, does this need?
6. **Recommendation:** which route, or neither, would you choose for a university lab making a few such parts per week, and when would each be the wrong choice? Compare briefly with buying cast master alloys or arc-melting a button from the weighed powders.

Abstract:
Abstract Metals and alloys are among the most technologically important materials for our industrialized societies. They are the most common structural materials used in cars, airplanes and buildings, and constitute the technological core of most electronic devices. They allow the transportation of energy over great distances and are exploited in critical parts of renewable energy technologies. Even though primary metal production industries are mature and operate optimized pyrometallurgical processes, they extensively rely on cheap and abundant carbonaceous reactants (fossil fuels, coke), require high power heating units (which are also typically powered by fossil fuels) to calcine, roast, smelt and refine, and they generate many output streams with high residual energy content. Many unit operations also generate hazardous gaseous species on top of large CO_2 emissions which require gas-scrubbing and capture strategies for the future. Therefore, there are still many opportunities to lower the environmental footprint of key pyrometallurgical operations. This paper explores the possibility to use greener reactants such as bio-fuels, bio-char, hydrogen and ammonia in different pyrometallurgical units. It also identifies all recycled streams that are available (such as steel and aluminum scraps, electronic waste and Li-ion batteries) as well as the technological challenges associated with their integration in primary metal processes. A complete discussion about the alternatives to carbon-based reduction is constructed around the use of hydrogen, metallo-reduction as well as inert anode electrometallurgy. The review work is completed with an overview of the different approaches to use renewable energies and valorize residual heat in pyrometallurgical units. Finally, strategies to mitigate environmental impacts of pyrometallurgical operations such as CO_2 capture utilization and storage as well as gas scrubbing technologies are detailed. This original review paper brings together for the first time all potential strategies and efforts that could be deployed in the future to decrease the environmental footprint of the pyrometallurgical industry. It is primarily intended to favour collaborative work and establish synergies between academia, the pyrometallurgical industry, decision-makers and equipment providers. Graphical abstract Highlights A more sustainable production of metals using greener reactants, green electricity or carbon capture is possible and sometimes already underway. More investments and pressure are required to hasten change. Discussion Is there enough pressure on the aluminum and steel industries to meet the set climate targets? The greenhouse gas emissions of existing facilities can often be partly mitigated by retrofitting them with green technologies, should we close plants prematurely to build new plants using greener technologies? Since green or renewable resources presently have limited availability, in which sector should we use them to maximize their benefits?

Abstract:
This overview paper describes the interaction of powder metallurgical iron-base alloys with the atmosphere during sintering. The methods of thermal analysis serve to clarify the processes that take place especially during the heating stage of the sintering cycle. After a discussion of the physical and chemical fundamentals of the sintering process, the methods of thermal analysis are explained. The differences between plain iron and alloyed systems are discussed in detail. Classical PM low alloy steels with alloying elements, such as Cu, Ni and Mo, react in a similar way as unalloyed carbon steels. The situation changes dramatically, when oxygen sensitive elements as chromium, manganese and even more silicon come into play. The removal of the surface oxygen is much more crucial, and there are several competing reactions, which have to be considered when these systems should be sintered in industrial scale to reach the desired mechanical and dimensional properties.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study presents a comprehensive characterization of recycled aluminum briquettes produced by cold pressing of Al–Si–Mg alloy machining chips, along with an evaluation of their behavior during subsequent remelting. The objective was to assess the density, porosity, chemical composition, and metallurgical yield of the briquettes before and after melting, as well as to determine their suitability for use as deoxidizing additives in steelmaking. The cold-pressed briquette (Sample A) exhibited a low density of 2.29 g.cm-³ and a porosity of 12.1%, resulting from intergranular voids and residual lubricants. After melting and resolidification (Sample B), the density increased to 2.388 g.cm-3 and the porosity decreased to 8.15%. XRF chemical analysis confirmed a high degree of elemental homogeneity after melting with no indication of segregation, while SEM–EDS microstructural analysis verified the absence of significant intermetallic phases and revealed only a thin surface oxide layer. The metallurgical yield reached 94.2% with a low dross content (2.25%). The results demonstrate that, following appropriate preprocessing and optimized compaction, recycled aluminum briquettes constitute a stable and efficient secondary aluminum material suitable for steel deoxidation, and they can significantly reduce the environmental impact of metallurgical production.</jats:p>

Abstract:

 This critical review examines advances in preprocessing and remelting processes for aluminium alloy chip recycling, emphasizing pre-treatment and remelting techniques that improve both resource recovery and material quality. Pre-treatment strategies, particularly cleaning methods and compaction are critically evaluated. Various cleaning methods, including centrifugation, ultrasonic solvent washing, extraction, and distillation are compared based on their ability to remove residual cutting fluids. Cold compaction, which augments chip density to approximately 2.5 g/cm³, significantly curtails oxidation losses and enhances metal recovery. During remelting, NaCl-KCl-based fluxes with limited fluoride additions (e.g., 3–7 wt% Na₃AlF₆) disrupt oxide networks but require careful dosage control to minimize furnace corrosion and environmental hazards. Moreover, mechanical stirring combined with suitable melting temperatures reduces porosity while enhancing melt purity. Future research should prioritize the development of low-energy cleaning methods, flux composition optimization, and scalable production techniques to further advance sustainable aluminium recycling.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Aluminum recycling is pivotal for achieving carbon neutrality and advancing the circular economy, offering significant reductions in energy use and greenhouse gas emissions compared to primary production. This review synthesizes global advances from 2020 to 2025 in scrap collection, sorting, remelting, and alloy recovery, with a focus on technological progress, sustainability metrics, and policy integration. Secondary aluminum already supplies over one-third of global demand and could surpass 50 % by 2030 with stronger segregation systems and extended producer responsibility (EPR) schemes. Innovations such as high-shear degassing, solid-state chip recycling, and chloride-free refining have improved melt quality and reduced salt-slag waste. At the same time, life-cycle assessments indicate up to 95% lower emissions compared to virgin aluminum. Persistent barriers remain—namely alloy contamination, inconsistent scrap classification, and limited traceability in informal collection networks. Regional policy experiences demonstrate that harmonized standards, mandatory recycled-content targets, and digital traceability accelerate market adaptation, whereas developing economies still face fragmented logistics and weak governance. Future directions include integrating real-time life-cycle assessment, artificial intelligence-based scrap sorting, and international alloy standards, enabling over 80% recycled content. Overall, aluminum recycling emerges as a technologically mature, economically competitive, and environmentally decisive route for decarbonizing metallurgical production and supporting the global energy transition.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Rotary furnaces remain important in secondary aluminum production because they can process oxidized, coated, low-density, contaminated, and dross-rich feeds that are difficult to recover in conventional bath furnaces. Their flexibility creates a recovery–residue trade-off: heat, rotation, and chloride–fluoride fluxes can liberate and coalesce metal droplets, but may also increase oxidation, emissions, refractory attack, and salt-slag generation. This structured critical narrative review evaluates a coded corpus of 106 publications from 2020 to August 2026. Retrospective A–E classification was performed by one reviewer and represents interpretive judgments of industrial transferability. No level-A repeated industrial campaign with closed aluminum–salt–energy–quality balances was identified. Accordingly, the proposed nine-gate Feedstock–Flux–Furnace–Residue framework is a testable decision architecture rather than a validated control model; low-salt and salt-free strategies remain feed-specific and require prospective industrial validation.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Ceramic matrix composites reinforced with carbon nanotubes are becoming increasingly popular in industry due to their astonishing mechanical properties and taking into account the fact that advanced production technologies make carbon nanotubes increasingly affordable. In the present paper, the most convenient contemporary methods used for the compaction of molding masses composed of either technical ceramics or ceramic matrix composites reinforced with carbon nanotubes are surveyed. This stage that precedes debinding and sintering plays the key role in getting pore-free equal-density ceramics at the scale of mass production. The methods include: compaction in sealed and collector molds, cold isostatic and quasi-isostatic compaction; dynamic compaction methods, such as magnetic pulse, vibration, and ultrasonic compaction; extrusion, stamping, and injection; casting from aqueous and non-aqueous slips; tape and gel casting. Capabilities of mold-free approaches to produce precisely shaped ceramic bodies are also critically analyzed, including green ceramic machining and additive manufacturing technologies.

Abstract:
We provide a systematic overview of the mechanochemical reactions of inorganic solids, notably simple binary compounds, such as oxides, nitrides, carbides, sulphides, phosphides, hydrides, borides, borane derivatives, and related systems. Whereas the solid state has been traditionally considered to be of little synthetic value by the broader community of synthetic chemists, the solid-state community, and in particular researchers focusing on the reactions of inorganic materials, have thrived in building a rich and dynamic research field based on mechanically-driven transformations of inorganic substances typically seen as inert and high-melting. This review provides an insight into the chemical richness of such mechanochemical reactions and, at the same time, offers their tentative categorisation based on transformation type, resulting in seven distinct groupings: (i) the formation of adducts, (ii) the reactions of dehydration; (iii) oxidation–reduction (redox) reactions; (iv) metathesis (or exchange) reactions; (v) doping and structural rearrangements, including reactions involving the reaction vessel (the milling jar); (vi) acid–base reactions, and (vii) other, mixed type reactions. At the same time, we offer a parallel description of inorganic mechanochemical reactions depending on the reaction conditions, as those that: (i) take place under mild conditions (e.g., manual grinding using a mortar and a pestle); (ii) proceed gradually under mechanical milling; (iii) are self-sustained and initiated by mechanical milling, i.e., mechanically induced self-propagating reactions (MSRs); and (iv) proceed only via harsh grinding and are a result of chemical reactivity under strongly non-equilibrium conditions. By elaborating on typical examples and general principles in the mechanochemistry of hard and high-melting substances, this review provides a suitable complement to the existing literature, focusing on the properties and mechanochemical reactions of inorganic solids, such as nanomaterials and catalysts.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Metal powders have both a high specific energy and a high energy density, which explains their widespread use in energetic materials (propellants, explosives and pyrotechnics). Pyrotechnic compositions are used extensively for both civilian and military applications. However, the combustion of pyrotechnics remains challenging to understand or predict due to the diversity of the components and the wide range of parameters that affect their results. Therefore, ongoing research efforts worldwide aim to investigate the combustion mechanisms of pyrotechnic compositions to improve their performance. In this review, studies on the ignition and combustion mechanisms of four metal powders (Al, Mg, Fe and B) are discussed. Moreover, their use as fuel in pyrotechnic systems is reported, as well as the combustion performance and energy release of the pyrotechnic mixtures. Additionally, some mixtures composed of fluorinated oxidizers and Al, Mg and B are also presented. Thermal analysis methods such as DSC and TG are used to obtain the thermal behavior of the pyrotechnic compositions. Furthermore, parameters such as particle size and the equivalence ratio that affect the performance of pyrotechnic mixtures and those that remain little studied are reported in this review.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000000

From text 'yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 2-4'.

Michiaki Yamasaki and Yoshihito Kawamura. Changes in the surface characteristics of gas-atomized pure aluminum powder during vacuum degassing. Materials Transactions, 47:1902-1905, Aug 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.2320/matertrans.47.1902, doi:10.2320/matertrans.47.1902. This article has 29 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Yamasaki and Kawamura directly measured water adsorption, temperature-programmed desorption (TPD), and XPS changes during vacuum degassing of gas-atomized pure aluminum powder (Materials Transactions 47, 1902–1905, 2006; DOI: 10.2320/matertrans.47.1902). The H2O-derived BET surface area was 0.125 m² g−1, and the adsorption isotherm showed a low-pressure hysteresis loop, interpreted as ultramicropores in the surface layer. Humid-air-exposed powder released H2O beginning near 480 K, with a peak near 720 K; H2O desorption was not detected after exposure to dry air or high-purity argon. Hydrogen evolution increased sharply at approximately 620 and 660 K and peaked at approximately 725 K, while no low-temperature H2 evolution was observed around 473 K. XPS indicated increasing dehydration and crystallization with temperature, with amorphous hydrated alumina transforming to crystalline α-Al2O3 at about 623 K. The authors distinguish this oxide transformation from later hydrogen release: oxidation of aluminum by hydration water produces chemisorbed surface hydrogen at 623 K, followed by recombination/desorption as H2 around 725 K. The excerpt does not provide numerical hydrogen volumes, absolute vacuum pressure, pore-closure measurements, or CIP-versus-die-pressing data.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 1-2'.

Michiaki Yamasaki and Yoshihito Kawamura. Changes in the surface characteristics of gas-atomized pure aluminum powder during vacuum degassing. Materials Transactions, 47:1902-1905, Aug 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.2320/matertrans.47.1902, doi:10.2320/matertrans.47.1902. This article has 29 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Yamasaki and Kawamura directly examined 99.99% rapidly solidified, gas-atomized pure Al powder with a mean particle diameter of approximately 25 µm. For temperature-programmed desorption (TPD), powders were exposed for 24 hours at room temperature to humid air (>40% moisture), dry air (<20 ppm moisture), or high-purity argon (<0.5 ppm oxygen and moisture), then heated at 5 K min−1 under 10−3 Pa vacuum while desorbed gases were analyzed by quadrupole mass spectrometry. The reported H2O adsorption-derived BET surface area was 0.125 m2 g−1. Hydrated-Al2O3 decomposition to crystalline Al2O3 occurred at 623 K, whereas hydrogen desorption occurred at 725 K, indicating separate reactions. In humid-air-exposed powder, H2 desorption increased sharply at approximately 620–660 K and peaked at 725 K; no H2 desorption was detected after dry-air or high-purity-argon exposure. ## pqac-00000003

From text 'sweet2014advancedsinteringtechniquesa pages 61-65'.

G Sweet. Advanced sintering techniques of aluminum: spark plasma sintering. Unknown journal, 2014.

The excerpt provides quantitative SPS degassing observations for aluminum and Al–0.4Mg powders, but it does not contain the requested direct Yamasaki (2006), Chua (2014), or Wei (2011) experiments, nor any DOI information. Under vacuum, moderate temperatures promote decomposition of hydrated surface phases, with degassing typically lasting hours. Physisorbed water is released below approximately 175°C; chemisorbed hydroxide/water-containing phases decompose over approximately 150–550°C. Hydrogen evolution begins above 200°C and peaks near 450°C. The cited reactions are aluminum hydrate decomposition to alumina and water, followed by aluminum/water reaction producing alumina and hydrogen; analogous magnesium reactions are also given. For SPS samples, initial oxygen contents were approximately 3000 ppm for Al and 1730 ppm for Al–0.4Mg, while initial hydrogen contents were approximately 69 and 54 ppm, respectively. Measured net oxygen-to-hydrogen loss ratios were 16:1–20:1 for Al and 16:1–27:1 for Al–0.4Mg, indicating excess oxygen release relative to the expected 8:1 water-loss ratio. In size-effect experiments, 20 mm specimens exceeded 99% relative density across the studied temperatures, whereas larger 80 mm slugs required higher temperatures. At 400°C residual gases increased; at temperatures ≥500°C both oxygen and hydrogen were substantially reduced. The passage discusses residual porosity and possible rehydration after vacuum removal, but does not quantify pore closure or trapped-gas volumes.

## pqac-00000004

From text 'chua2014developmentofaluminuma pages 95-98'.

AS Chua. Development of aluminum powder metallurgy alloys for aerospace applications. Unknown journal, 2014.

This excerpt provides quantitative results for spark plasma sintering (SPS) of PM2024 and PM7075 aluminum alloy powders, not gas-atomized pure aluminum. At a 400°C peak temperature, SPS samples reached greater than 99.5% theoretical density. In the T6 temper, reported apparent hardness values were 71 HRB for PM2024 and 87 HRB for PM7075. SPS produced substantial reductions in residual oxygen and hydrogen, with evolved-gas analysis attributing the reductions principally to release of CO2 and adsorbed/chemisorbed H2O. Trace oxygen was also consumed by temperature-dependent self-gettering at particle surfaces, partially reversing oxygen removal; the excerpt states that this gettering response was broadly consistent between the powders. Particle size affected processing: particles with nominal size at least 180 µm gave enhanced densification and minimized O/H impurities. Figure 4.15 compares oxygen loss for 180 µm and 45 µm particles in both alloys, but the excerpt does not provide numerical oxygen-loss values. It contains no Yamasaki 2006 data on pure aluminum hydroxide decomposition, hydrogen volumes, vacuum degassing, or temperature-specific gas evolution; no CIP-versus-die-pressure comparison; no trapped-gas or pore-closure measurements; and no DOI. The cited information therefore supports only limited Chua 2014 SPS density, hardness, gas-release, and particle-size context.

Abstract:
Bimetals—materials composed of two metal components with dissimilar standard reduction–oxidation (redox) potentials—offer unique electronic, optical, and catalytic properties, surpassing monometallic systems. These materials exhibit not only the combined attributes of their constituent metals but also new and novel properties arising from their synergy. Although many reviews have explored the synthesis, properties, and applications of bimetallic systems, none have focused exclusively on iron (Fe)- and aluminum (Al)-based bimetals. This systematic review addresses this gap by providing a comprehensive overview of conventional and emerging techniques for Fe-based and Al-based bimetal synthesis. Specifically, this work systematically reviewed recent studies from 2014 to 2023 using the Scopus, Web of Science (WoS), and Google Scholar databases, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, and was registered under INPLASY with the registration number INPLASY202540026. Articles were excluded if they were inaccessible, non-English, review articles, conference papers, book chapters, or not directly related to the synthesis of Fe- or Al-based bimetals. Additionally, a bibliometric analysis was performed to evaluate the research trends on the synthesis of Fe-based and Al-based bimetals. Based on the 122 articles analyzed, Fe-based and Al-based bimetal synthesis methods were classified into three types: (i) physical, (ii) chemical, and (iii) biological techniques. Physical methods include mechanical alloying, radiolysis, sonochemical methods, the electrical explosion of metal wires, and magnetic field-assisted laser ablation in liquid (MF-LAL). In comparison, chemical protocols covered reduction, dealloying, supported particle methods, thermogravimetric methods, seed-mediated growth, galvanic replacement, and electrochemical synthesis. Meanwhile, biological techniques utilized plant extracts, chitosan, alginate, and cellulose-based materials as reducing agents and stabilizers during bimetal synthesis. Research works on the synthesis of Fe-based and Al-based bimetals initially declined but increased in 2018, followed by a stable trend, with 50% of the total studies conducted in the last five years. China led in the number of publications (62.3%), followed by Russia, Australia, and India, while Saudi Arabia had the highest number of citations per document (95). RSC Advances was the most active journal, publishing eight papers from 2014 to 2023, while Applied Catalysis B: Environmental had the highest number of citations per document at 203. Among the three synthesis methods, chemical techniques dominated, particularly supported particles, galvanic replacement, and chemical reduction, while biological and physical methods have started gaining interest. Iron–copper (Fe/Cu), iron–aluminum (Fe/Al), and iron–nickel (Fe/Ni) were the most commonly synthesized bimetals in the last 10 years. Finally, this work was funded by DOST-PCIEERD and DOST-ERDT.

## 2. Mechanical characterization of high volume fraction Al7075-Al_2O_3 composite fabricated by semisolid powder processing

Abstract:
The mechanical properties and physical characteristics of aluminum alloy composites can be significantly improved by adding reinforcing phases. However, the high loading of the reinforcement phase in Al7075-Al_2O_3 composites has not been thoroughly studied. In this work, a combination of semisolid metal powder processing and powder metallurgy is used to process and manufacture Al7075-Al_2O_3 composites with a high reinforcement fraction of > 40 vol.%. The effects of processing parameters on the microstructures and mechanical properties of the composite material are discussed in detail. The loading limits of the high volume Al_2O_3 reinforcement in Al7075 composites are identified and linked to the processing parameters. A methodology is introduced to estimate the consolidation temperature of Al7075 alloy using compaction testing. Al_2O_3 particles (the average particle size of 120 µm) were mechanically milled with Al7075 powder (the average particle size of 20 µm) for 10 min and 5 h using a high-energy planetary ball mill. The mixture was then compacted in the semisolid state at 615 °C under the compaction pressures of 50 MPa and 100 MPa. By increasing the milling time from 10 min to 5 h, the deformation of aluminum powders and the fracture of Al_2O_3 reinforcement particles occur, restricting the loading limit of reinforcement. The milling time also shows a dominant effect on the powder morphology, microstructure, and mechanical properties of Al7075-Al_2O_3 composites. Increasing compaction pressure from 50 to 100 MPa significantly improved the compressive strength of the composite from 218 to 652 MPa. Al7075-Al_2O_3 composite with 40 vol.% of reinforcing phase exhibits the highest hardness of 198.2 HV and 96.9% relative density when it is milled for 5 h and compacted at 100 MPa. However, this composite shows the highest strength of 652 MPa when it is milled for 10 min. By increasing the reinforcing phase to 50 vol.% and 60 vol.%, the hardness, density, and compressive strength of composites decreased. The composites with 60 vol.% of reinforcing phase appeared overloaded. Results show that semisolid metal powder processing has huge potential for the fabrication of high loading Al_2O_3 in Al7075 matrix with near theoretical density.

Abstract:
In powder metallurgy (PM), severe plastic deformation (SPD) is a well-known technological solution to achieve interesting properties. However, the occurrence of pores in the final product may limit these properties. Also, for a given type of microstructure, the stereometric parameters of the pore structures, such as shape (represented by Aspect and Dcircle) and distribution (fshape, and fcircle), decisively affect the final properties. The influence of different processing routes (pressing, sintering and equal channel angular pressing (ECAP)) on pore structures in an aluminum PM alloy is discussed. The nature of porosity, porosity evolution and its behavior is explored. The correlation between pore size and morphology is also considered. The final pore structure parameters (Aspect, Dcircle, fshape, and fcircle) of studied aluminum alloys produced by different processing routes depends on the different formation routes.

Abstract:
In recent years, closed-cell porous Aluminum (Al) has drawn increasing attention, particularly in the applications requiring reduced weight and energy absorption capability such as in the automotive and aerospace industries. In the present work, porous Al with closed-cell structure was successfully fabricated by powder metallurgy technique using PMMA as a space holder. The effects of the amount of PMMA powder on the porosity, density, microstructure and compressive behaviors of the porous specimens were systematically evaluated. The results showed that closed-cell porous Al having different porosities (12%–32%) and densities (1.6478 g/cm3, 1.5125 g/cm3 and 1.305 g/cm3) could be produced by varying the amount of PMMA (20–30 wt %). Meanwhile, the compressive behavior results demonstrated that the plateau stress decreased and the energy absorption capacity increased with increasing amount of PMMA. However, the maximum energy absorption capacity was achieved in the closed-cell porous Al with the addition of 25 wt % PMMA. Therefore, fabrication of closed-cell porous Al using 25 wt % PMMA is considered as the optimal condition in the present study since the resultant closed-cell porous Al possessed good combinations of porosity, density and plateau stress, as well as energy absorption capacity.

These methods allow fabricating parts with smooth surfaces and improved mechanical characteristics—porosity, tensile strength. Application of the traditional design set-up with a single-axial loading is restricted to high stresses in the dies to deform the preforms that lead to cracks formation. Abstract:
<jats:p>The Ni-Al system contains five intermetallic compounds, out of which NiAl and Ni3Al have received the vast majority of scientific and industrial interest over the past few decades. Ni3Al is of major interest due to its unique properties, including a yield strength that increases with temperature. The combustion synthesis (CS) process for producing Ni3Al from elemental powders of nickel and aluminum offers a low thermal budget and rapid processing, as well as purer products. This paper reviews the fundamentals of CS as applied to Ni3Al and its composites, and focuses on research over the past 25 years, including mechanically and electrically activated combustion synthesis and combined combustion synthesis and bulk deformation processes to produce high-density products. Several new directions are suggested for future research in the field.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000005

From text 'eksi2007effectofsintering pages 4-5'.

A.K. Eksi and A.H. Yuzbasioglu. Effect of sintering and pressing parameters on the densification of cold isostatically pressed al and fe powders. Materials & Design, 28:1364-1368, Jan 2007. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2006.01.018, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2006.01.018. This article has 49 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports cold-isostatic pressing and sintering results for aluminum and iron powders. For soft aluminum, near-full densification was obtained at 400 MPa, while plastic deformation began above 100 MPa. The reported maximum sintered aluminum density was 99.3% at 600 MPa, followed by sintering at 600 °C for 20 minutes. The text states that aluminum density increased by only 1.5% during sintering, indicating that most densification occurred during pressing. For iron, plastic deformation began above 300 MPa; approximately 89% density was achieved at 600 MPa before sintering. The maximum reported sintered iron density was 91.5% at 600 MPa and 1200 °C for 30 minutes, although the body of the excerpt also reports a maximum of 90.3% at 1200 °C/30 minutes, suggesting a possible distinction or inconsistency between plotted and concluding values. Iron density increased by only 1.74% after sintering. SEM observations describe reduced porosity and complete plastic deformation at high pressure. The excerpt gives no numerical pore-size measurements, oxide analysis, green-strength values, or information about the Andasmas 2011 Al–Ni study; therefore oxide effects and direct comparison with that work cannot be established from this passage.

## pqac-00000006

From text 'eksi2007effectofsintering pages 1-2'.

A.K. Eksi and A.H. Yuzbasioglu. Effect of sintering and pressing parameters on the densification of cold isostatically pressed al and fe powders. Materials & Design, 28:1364-1368, Jan 2007. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2006.01.018, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2006.01.018. This article has 49 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports a cold-isostatic-pressing study of aluminum and iron powders, but it does not specifically identify the aluminum as “pure,” nor does it provide the requested detailed pore-size measurements, oxide characterization, green strength data, or the Andasmas et al. (2011) Al–Ni comparison. The stated CIP pressure was up to 600 MPa. Initial packing densities were 48% for Al and 33% for Fe; after pressing at 600 MPa, the reported relative densities were 98% for Al and 89.2% for Fe. Aluminum specimens were sintered under argon at 600, 620, and 640 °C for 20 minutes. Iron specimens were sintered at 1200 °C for 30, 60, and 90 minutes. The maximum reported post-sintering densifications were 99.3% for Al at 600 °C for 20 minutes and 91.5% for Fe at 1200 °C for 30 minutes. The article describes sintering as pore removal accompanied by particle growth and bonding, and notes that shrinkage can cause cracking and distortion. The methods excerpt indicates that density was measured before and after CIP and after sintering, using a copper tube container and argon-controlled furnace conditions. No direct evidence here supports conclusions about oxide effects, pore-size distributions, green strength, or the 2011 Al–Ni study.

## pqac-00000007

From text 'eksi2007effectofsintering pages 2-4'.

A.K. Eksi and A.H. Yuzbasioglu. Effect of sintering and pressing parameters on the densification of cold isostatically pressed al and fe powders. Materials & Design, 28:1364-1368, Jan 2007. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2006.01.018, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2006.01.018. This article has 49 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides experimental conditions and qualitative density results for Eksi and Yuzbasioglu (2007), but not enough readable numerical data to report exact green relative densities or sintered densities from the plots. Compaction-pressure graphs span approximately 100–600 MPa, and the text specifically states that cold welding between particles occurred in nonsintered aluminium specimens pressed at 100 MPa or above; for iron, the corresponding threshold was 300 MPa or above, attributed to plastic deformation. Aluminium parts were sintered at 600, 620, and 640 °C for 20 minutes, with heating at 5 °C/min and controlled argon cooling. Iron parts were sintered at 1200 °C for 30, 60, and 90 minutes. The powder size range is reported as 150 + 106 µm (apparently indicating the 106–150 µm fraction), while the listed apparent densities are 50% for gas-atomized aluminium and 35% for water-atomized iron. The passage discusses pressure-assisted pore elimination in general, noting that external pressure is most effective during later sintering stages, but it gives no specific pore sizes or direct analysis of oxide effects. It also contains no information about Andasmas (2011), aluminium–nickel CIP densities, green strength, or oxide behavior.

## pqac-00000008

From text 'andasmas2011phenomenologicalstudyof pages 4-6'.

This article has 12 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt is relevant to the Andasmas et al. (2011) aluminum–nickel cold-isostatic-pressing comparison, but it does not provide the requested Eksi Yuzbasioglu (2007) results for pure aluminum, nor information on sintering temperatures, pore sizes, iron comparison, or oxide effects. For pure Al in the Andasmas study, the Shapiro–Kolthoff analysis separates particle rearrangement from plastic deformation; Table 2 gives a first transition pressure of 190.6 MPa, while Table 3 reports the Al rearrangement slope as KA1 = 9.355 × 10−3 and the plastic-deformation slope as KA3 = 2.622 × 10−3. The mixtures have first/second transitions of 188.6/595.8 MPa for Ni+Al and 243.9/400.1 MPa for 3Ni+Al. The authors interpret the intermediate mixture slope as aluminum plastic deformation plus the end of nickel rearrangement, followed by nickel plastic deformation. Aluminum, identified as the softer element, deforms before nickel. Williamson–Hall results indicate increasing lattice/micro-distortion with pressure, especially in aluminum. Hardness decreases strongly when aluminum is added, with reductions reported at 400, 600, and 800 MPa. The only explicit green relative-density value in the excerpt is 94.15% for a compact CIPed at 800 MPa. Green strength is not directly reported, although hardness is discussed as structural characterization and for estimating extrusion pressure.

This excerpt provides limited information relevant to the comparison of cold-isostatic pressing (CIP) of aluminum and nickel powders. In the Andasmas et al. study, compaction pressure plateaus ranged from 50 to 1000 MPa, with plateau times of one minute used to improve density homogeneity; preliminary rapid depressurization produced a high-density surface and low-density core. Geometrically measured compact densities showed that most densification occurred during CIP, and pure aluminum reached more than 95% of its theoretical density. The authors describe two densification stages: low-pressure particle rearrangement, sliding, and restacking, followed after yielding by plastic deformation and permanent particle-shape changes. The table excerpt gives an aluminum transition pressure of 190.6 MPa from rearrangement to plastic deformation, with no second transition listed. The passage does not report green strength, pore sizes, sintering temperatures, oxide effects, or direct comparisons with iron. It also does not provide a complete pressure-density dataset or explicit absolute green densities for the Al-Ni mixtures. Therefore, it can support general CIP densification behavior and the cited aluminum transition pressure, but not the requested detailed Eksi Yuzbasioglu (2007) results or oxide-related conclusions.
