Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000016

From text 'kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 2-4'.

L. Kowalski, B. M. Korevaar, and J. Duszczyk. Some new aspects of the theory of oxidation and degassing of aluminium-based alloy powders. Journal of Materials Science, 27:2770-2780, Jan 1992. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00540704, doi:10.1007/bf00540704. This article has 52 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides useful baseline hydrogen and water-related information for gas-atomized aluminium alloy powders. Total hydrogen was reported as 24.5 ppm for air-atomized Al-Si-Cu-Mg powder and 19.8 ppm for nitrogen-atomized Al-Fe-Mo-Zr powder. Because these values greatly exceed hydrogen solubility in solid or molten aluminium (0.035 and 0.7 ppm, respectively), the authors infer that nearly all hydrogen is associated with the oxide layer, either as hydroxides or physically adsorbed water vapour, rather than dissolved hydrogen in the metal. Comparison with oxygen content, oxide thickness (approximately 5–7 nm), and powder surface area led them to conclude that the hydrogen quantity is sufficient to saturate the oxide’s outer layer with water. The excerpt also distinguishes atmospheric exposure: humid air can cause oxidation and bind water at the surface as hydrated alumina or physically adsorbed water. For degassing, compacted powder was heated under high vacuum at approximately 2.5 °C min−1 to above the hydrogen-evolution peak, while water and hydrogen were monitored by mass spectrometry. Samples were then exposed to normal atmosphere for 24 hours and degassed again. Exact evolved-water quantities, vacuum pressure, hold times, and complete desorption-temperature ranges are not given here; the air-atomized hydrogen curve is only shown to begin with a peak near 175 °C.


---

## pqac-00000017

From text 'estrada1991gasentrapmentand pages 6-8'.

J. L. Estrada, J. Duszczyk, and B. M. Korevaar. Gas entrapment and evolution in prealloyed aluminium powders. Journal of Materials Science, 26:1431-1442, Mar 1991. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00544650, doi:10.1007/bf00544650. This article has 38 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Estrada, Duszczyk, and Korevaar report hydrogen released from two air-atomized aluminium-alloy powders: powder J1 contained 24.58 ppm H, equivalent to 27.53 mL per 100 g, while K1 contained 13.09 ppm H, equivalent to 14.66 mL per 100 g. These values were measured at 550 °C and are stated to be 50–100 times higher than hydrogen levels in degassed cast alloys. The authors conclude that practically all measured hydrogen resides in the particle oxide layer as chemically or physically bound H2O, rather than as dissolved hydrogen in the aluminium matrix. The proposed degassing chemistry includes removal of adsorbed water vapour, dehydration of hydrated surface oxides/hydroxides (Al2O3·3H2O → Al2O3 + H2O), oxide formation involving oxygen, and reactions of aluminium or magnesium with water that produce molecular H2. Thus, the excerpt distinguishes adsorbed moisture and hydroxide/oxide-bound water conceptually, but does not provide separate numerical amounts for each fraction or a direct dissolved-H measurement. Vacuum degassing was tested from 20 to 550 °C at approximately 2.5 °C/min. Powder was cold-compacted at 160 MPa to about 65% theoretical density, leaving interconnected porosity. A turbomolecular-pump/quadrupole-mass-spectrometer system monitored released gases, but this excerpt gives no numerical vacuum pressure, dwell time, or discrete desorption-temperature ranges. It also contains no data from Kowalski 1992, Davis 1995, or Yamasaki 2004.


---

## pqac-00000018

From text 'davis1995degassingandsurface pages 1-2'.

S. J. Davis, A. P. Miodownik, and J. F. Watts. Degassing and surface analysis of gas atomized aluminium alloy powders. Journal of Materials Science, 30:3811-3819, Aug 1995. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01153939, doi:10.1007/bf01153939. This article has 13 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt from Davis, Miodownik, and Watts (1995) provides qualitative and temperature-resolved evidence for separating water species and hydrogen during degassing of gas-atomized aluminium-alloy powders, but it does not report absolute evolved quantities in mass percent, ppm, or mL per 100 g, nor does the excerpt specify vacuum pressure or degassing duration. It identifies an early desorption feature attributed to adsorbed water at approximately 100 °C. Chemically bonded or oxide/hydroxide-associated water is released at higher temperatures, with prior work cited as observing water evolution mainly between 120 and 200 °C. Hydrogen evolution occurs at substantially higher temperatures, typically about 350–450 °C, with a cited maximum near 400 °C; another cited result reports a water maximum near 200 °C. The text links hydrogen evolution to a rapid decline in the water signal, suggesting reaction of water-related surface species with alloy or surface components. The paper also reports greater hydrogen evolution for larger particle-size fractions and discusses carbonate decomposition with CO2 evolution. Complete degassing is described as requiring heating to the highest temperature compatible with avoiding structural degradation; prolonged treatment at lower temperature may be insufficient. Estrada (1991), Kowalski (1992), and Yamasaki (2004) are not covered in this excerpt, so their quantitative gas yields, pressures, and times cannot be extracted here.


---

## pqac-00000019

From text 'estrada1991gasentrapmentand pages 5-6'.

J. L. Estrada, J. Duszczyk, and B. M. Korevaar. Gas entrapment and evolution in prealloyed aluminium powders. Journal of Materials Science, 26:1431-1442, Mar 1991. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00544650, doi:10.1007/bf00544650. This article has 38 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Estrada et al. (1991) distinguishes several gas-containing surface reservoirs in atomized aluminium powders. The particles have a hydrated oxide film containing both adsorbed water and hydroxide-bound water, described for aluminium as A1203·2Al(OH)3 and for magnesium-containing alloys as MgO–Mg(OH)2 mixtures, with physically adsorbed H2O/O2. The excerpt identifies progressive hydroxide/oxyhydroxide dehydration transformations over approximately 150–175 °C, 310–500 °C, and above 500 °C, but it does not provide numerical water or hydrogen yields in mass percent, ppm, or mL per 100 g. During heating, absorbed water is removed first; hydrogen can also arise from desorption of absorbed or dissolved hydrogen. At higher temperature, especially above about 400 °C, water reacts with oxide-free aluminium and magnesium, producing hydrogen through 2Al + 3H2O → Al2O3 + 3H2 and Mg + H2O → MgO + H2. Magnesium hydroxide and MgAl2O4 are noted as relatively stable and complicating degassing. Degassing effectiveness depends on equilibrium gas pressure, diffusion, surface reactions, temperature, and time; the cited relation gives concentration change as dependent on pressure and time and inversely on material thickness. No explicit vacuum pressure or degassing-time dataset is included in these pages.


---

## pqac-00000020

From text 'yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 1-2'.

Michiaki Yamasaki and Yoshihito Kawamura. Changes in the surface characteristics of gas-atomized pure aluminum powder during vacuum degassing. Materials Transactions, 47:1902-1905, Aug 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.2320/matertrans.47.1902, doi:10.2320/matertrans.47.1902. This article has 29 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt provides temperature and experimental-condition data relevant to quantifying water and hydrogen evolution from gas-atomized aluminum powder, but it does not report the evolved quantities in mass percent, ppm, or mL per 100 g. For temperature-programmed desorption, powders were heated at 5 K min−1 under 10−3 Pa vacuum, with desorbed gases analyzed continuously by quadrupole mass spectrometry. Powder exposure conditions included humid air (>40% moisture), dry air (<20 ppm moisture), and high-purity argon (<0.5 ppm oxygen and moisture), following 24-hour room-temperature exposure. Water desorption was measured separately, but numerical H2O amounts and desorption-temperature values are not included in the supplied pages. The excerpt distinguishes surface-adsorbed gases and water from chemically bound water in hydrated alumina/aluminum hydroxide. Hydrated-Al2O3 decomposition to crystalline Al2O3 occurred at 623 K, while hydrogen desorption occurred at approximately 620–660 K onset/increase and peaked at 725 K. Hydrogen was observed after humid-air exposure but not after dry-air or argon exposure, supporting a relationship to moisture-derived surface species. The proposed reactions separate oxide hydration conversion from subsequent hydrogen evolution: hydrated alumina reacts with aluminum to form crystalline alumina and surface hydrogen, followed by recombination of surface hydrogen into H2. No information on Estrada 1991, Kowalski 1992, Davis 1995, or Yamasaki 2004 appears in this excerpt.


---

## pqac-00000021

From text 'yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 2-4'.

Michiaki Yamasaki and Yoshihito Kawamura. Changes in the surface characteristics of gas-atomized pure aluminum powder during vacuum degassing. Materials Transactions, 47:1902-1905, Aug 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.2320/matertrans.47.1902, doi:10.2320/matertrans.47.1902. This article has 29 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt provides qualitative and temperature-resolved evidence relevant to quantifying surface water and hydrogen evolution from gas-atomized pure aluminum, but it does not report mass percentages, ppm, mL per 100 g, vacuum pressure, or degassing duration. Water desorption from powder exposed to humid air began near 480 K and peaked near 720 K; no H2O desorption was detected after exposure to high-purity argon. The authors distinguish three water reservoirs: physically adsorbed water on the outer surface, water retained on pore walls, and chemisorbed water associated with hydrated aluminum oxide. A low-pressure hysteresis loop in the adsorption isotherm indicates ultramicropores, whose retained water requires higher-temperature outgassing. XPS indicates conversion of amorphous trihydrated alumina to crystalline alumina around 623 K. Hydrogen evolution is attributed to reaction of aluminum with hydrated oxide, but the oxidation/decomposition and hydrogen-release steps are separated: hydrated oxide reacts around 623 K to produce chemisorbed surface hydrogen, while Hsurf recombines and desorbs as H2 around 725 K. The excerpt therefore helps distinguish adsorbed water, oxide-bound water, and chemisorbed hydrogen, while additional cited studies (Estrada 1991, Kowalski 1992, Davis 1995, and Yamasaki 2004) would be needed for quantitative loading, pressure, and time data.


---

## pqac-00000022

From text 'davis1995degassingandsurface pages 3-5'.

S. J. Davis, A. P. Miodownik, and J. F. Watts. Degassing and surface analysis of gas atomized aluminium alloy powders. Journal of Materials Science, 30:3811-3819, Aug 1995. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01153939, doi:10.1007/bf01153939. This article has 13 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The Davis (1995) excerpt provides experimental conditions and qualitative temperature assignments relevant to quantifying water and hydrogen evolution from gas-atomized aluminium powders, but the supplied pages do not provide numerical mass-percent, ppm, or mL per 100 g values; those would need to be extracted from the complete figures, calibration data, or tables. Powders were exposed to continuously pumped UHV, with pressure reaching approximately 10^-5 mbar after about 14 h; an overnight 12 h pumpdown was standardized because 12–72 h pumping substantially reduced water evolution by removing physically bonded water. The powder was heated from ambient temperature to 560 °C at approximately 3.7 °C min^-1, while evolved gases were monitored by partial pressure. Water desorption at roughly 100–180 °C is associated with physically absorbed or increasingly chemisorbed surface water. Chemisorbed water introduced during atomization is reported to evolve only at higher temperatures. In Mg-containing alloys, hydrogen evolution becomes pronounced above approximately 400 °C and coincides with a sharp decline in the water signal, supporting the surface reaction Mg + H2O → MgO + H2. Thus, the observed high-temperature hydrogen cannot automatically be treated as dissolved hydrogen; in this excerpt it is principally interpreted as hydrogen generated by reaction of water with magnesium. Oxide-bound water and independently dissolved hydrogen are not quantitatively separated here.

## pqac-00000023

From text 'estrada1991gasentrapmentand pages 1-2'.

J. L. Estrada, J. Duszczyk, and B. M. Korevaar. Gas entrapment and evolution in prealloyed aluminium powders. Journal of Materials Science, 26:1431-1442, Mar 1991. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00544650, doi:10.1007/bf00544650. This article has 38 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt establishes the categories and qualitative behavior needed for comparison with Estrada (1991), Kowalski (1992), Davis (1995), and Yamasaki (2004), but it does not provide the requested evolved quantities in mass percent, ppm, or mL per 100 g, nor explicit vacuum-degassing times or pressure schedules. For Estrada’s AI-20Si-X powders, moisture and hydrogen partial pressures during degassing up to 550 °C were reported within 10^-4 to 10^-7 mbar. Temperature was identified as the critical parameter governing desorption. The excerpt distinguishes physically adsorbed water from chemically bound surface water: hydration produces hydroxides or oxy-hydroxides, while water and oxygen may also be physically adsorbed on powder surfaces. Vacuum degassing removes moisture, adsorbed hydrogen, and oxygen, and decomposes hydrated oxides; it also converts ductile aluminum hydroxide toward crystalline alumina. Magnesium-containing surface films shift moisture and hydrogen evolution toward higher temperatures because MgO is present alongside or instead of Al2O3. The passage also notes that magnesium reacts with water vapor more intensely than aluminum. Quantitative gas-evolution values, desorption intervals for separate species, and dissolved-hydrogen measurements must therefore be obtained from the full papers, especially their experimental results and tables.

## pqac-00000024

From text 'puga2009recyclingofaluminium pages 5-7'.

H. Puga, J. Barbosa, D. Soares, F. Silva, and S. Ribeiro. Recycling of aluminium swarf by direct incorporation in aluminium melts. Journal of Materials Processing Technology, 209:5195-5203, Jun 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2009.03.007, doi:10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2009.03.007. This article has 136 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt provides direct evidence for remelting aluminium machining swarf formed into briquettes in an induction furnace, but it does not report aluminium powder, separate chip geometries, preheating, fluxed versus flux-free operation, stirring conditions, or post-remelting mechanical properties. The tested charge used ingot to form an initial molten pool, followed by swarf briquettes. The selected conditions were approximately 15 kg total charge, 33.3% initial ingot/molten pool and 66.7% swarf briquettes compacted at 300 bar, induction melting at 850 °C under argon for 60 minutes. At 300 bar, experiments produced about 88.2–91.3% metal incorporation, with 8.0–8.9% dross; at 400 bar, incorporation was 81.3–85.4% and dross 11.7–13.5%; at 500 bar, incorporation fell to 75.0–78.3% and dross rose to 14.6–18.8%. Higher compaction reduced briquette porosity, hindered molten-metal penetration, increased melting time, and apparently left metal in the dross. Argon increased average recovery from 60.8% to 83.3% and reduced oxidation and dross. Larger initial molten pools produced approximately 90% recovery, whereas pools near 20% yielded around 85% or lower. The excerpt mentions plunging compacted swarf but gives no quantified stirring or immersion/preheating comparison.


---

## pqac-00000025

From text 'puga2009recyclingofaluminium pages 4-5'.

H. Puga, J. Barbosa, D. Soares, F. Silva, and S. Ribeiro. Recycling of aluminium swarf by direct incorporation in aluminium melts. Journal of Materials Processing Technology, 209:5195-5203, Jun 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2009.03.007, doi:10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2009.03.007. This article has 136 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt provides direct evidence for remelting compacted aluminium machining swarf briquettes, including induction-furnace trials, but it does not report aluminium powder, loose chips, fluxed briquettes, or a direct powder-versus-chip comparison. Briquette density increased with compaction pressure from 2.03 kg/dm3 at 300 bar to 2.10 kg/dm3 at 500 bar, while moisture decreased from 2.83% to 2.42%. In induction melting with 33.3% briquettes, metal incorporation was 85.1% at 850 °C and 83.3% at 800 °C, with dross of 9.6% and 11.4% of briquette mass, respectively. Resistance-furnace results were poorer: 68.8% and 62.5% incorporation, with 27.1–32.3% dross. Argon protection improved recovery to 81.3–85.4%, compared with 58.7–62.0% without protection, and reduced dross from 32.5–34.8% to 11.7–13.5%. Between 800 and 950 °C, recovery was approximately 79.5–85.2% and dross 11.6–15.5%; above 850 °C, recovery and dross changed little, although melting time fell from 65 minutes at 800 °C to 50 minutes at 950 °C. The excerpt attributes induction effects to electromagnetic stirring, which can increase hydrogen pickup, oxidation, and transient element loss, but gives no quantitative immersion/preheating comparison, flux-use comparison, or final-property data.

## pqac-00000026

From text 'puga2009recyclingofaluminium pages 1-2'.

H. Puga, J. Barbosa, D. Soares, F. Silva, and S. Ribeiro. Recycling of aluminium swarf by direct incorporation in aluminium melts. Journal of Materials Processing Technology, 209:5195-5203, Jun 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2009.03.007, doi:10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2009.03.007. This article has 136 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt provides direct evidence for recycling aluminium machining swarf in induction melts, but not for aluminium powder or briquetted swarf specifically. It states that recycling performance depends on swarf conditioning, melting technique, and metal-treatment methodology. The identified critical measures are reducing chip moisture, induction melting under a protective atmosphere, and applying a specially developed degassing technique. The process reportedly achieved approximately 90% metal recovery with minimum dross formation and without traditional salts or fluxes. The excerpt does not provide quantitative comparisons of immersion versus preheating, melt time, melt temperature, stirring intensity, or charge-addition procedure. It also does not distinguish powder from chips, report briquette behavior, or compare fluxed and flux-free conditions beyond identifying the developed process as flux-free. The material-specific challenges are important: swarf has low bulk density (0.25 kg/dm3), an aluminium-oxide film, and machining-fluid contamination. Without suitable preparation, the text predicts low recovery, high energy use, smoke and gas generation, inclusions, porosity, and poor mechanical properties. In contrast, the developed treatment produced AlSi12Cu1 ingots with microstructure, soundness, and chemical composition similar to commercial second-melt material. Traditional recovery may lose up to 50% of the aluminium.


---

## pqac-00000027

From text 'baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 5-7'.

Petr Baron, Jozef Mikita, and Vladimír Simkulet. Characterization of cold-pressed aluminum briquettes and their behavior during remelting for application in steel deoxidation. Unknown journal, Apr 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202604.0191.v1, doi:10.20944/preprints202604.0191.v1.

The excerpt provides direct evidence only for remelting a cold-pressed, flux-free aluminum machining-chip briquette in an induction furnace; it does not report a powder charge, loose machining swarf, fluxed briquettes, or a controlled comparison among these feed forms. The chips originated from AlSi and AlMgSi machining alloys and were mechanically cleaned, centrifuged to remove lubricants and coolant, and magnetically separated to remove ferromagnetic contaminants. They were cold pressed without binders at 100–160 MPa into approximately 322.8 g cylindrical briquettes. For remelting, the briquette was heated in an induction furnace to about 850 °C and cast into a mold, producing a 251.9 g remelted block. The stated rationale is that high density and low porosity reduce oxidation and fine-particle losses and improve aluminum recovery; the cited expected yield is 80–90%, depending on melting method. The excerpt does not quantify immersion versus preheating, melt time, stirring conditions, temperature history beyond approximately 850 °C, oxide/dross mass, metal yield measured for this trial, alloy-property changes, or mixing uniformity results. It mentions chemical homogeneity evaluation using six cross-sectional measurement points, but the reported analytical outcomes are not included in the supplied pages. Thus, it supports qualitative advantages of compacted chips but cannot distinguish powder behavior or quantify comparative remelting performance.

## pqac-00000028

From text 'puga2009recyclingofaluminium pages 2-3'.

H. Puga, J. Barbosa, D. Soares, F. Silva, and S. Ribeiro. Recycling of aluminium swarf by direct incorporation in aluminium melts. Journal of Materials Processing Technology, 209:5195-5203, Jun 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2009.03.007, doi:10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2009.03.007. This article has 136 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt provides direct evidence for remelting machining aluminium swarf in an induction melt, but not aluminium powder. The swarf was conditioned by 12 h decanting, centrifugation for 10 min at 400 rpm, and compaction into approximately 50 × 50 × 90 mm briquettes at 300, 400, or 500 bar. Briquettes were fed mechanically into a 5 kg AlSi12Cu1 molten bath using an automatic feeder designed to immerse them fully and prevent contact with the furnace atmosphere. The total melt stock was approximately 15 kg, and induction-furnace melting after the first briquette insertion took 50–70 min. Experiments evaluated 800, 850, 900, and 950 °C, with 33.3% briquettes in most tests and up to 80% in others; argon-protected and unprotected atmospheres were compared. The excerpt does not report stirring conditions, metal yield/recovery results, oxide or dross quantities, final properties, or explicit mixing-quality measurements. It describes conventional flux-assisted recovery as involving chloride salts and fluorides that break oxide films but generate hazardous salt-cake, while the reported induction procedure does not state that flux was used. Thus, the passage supports a comparison of briquetted machining swarf immersion, conditioning, temperature, and melt time, but supplies no powder-versus-chip comparison or quantitative outcome data.

## pqac-00000029

From text 'baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 18-20'.

Petr Baron, Jozef Mikita, and Vladimír Simkulet. Characterization of cold-pressed aluminum briquettes and their behavior during remelting for application in steel deoxidation. Unknown journal, Apr 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202604.0191.v1, doi:10.20944/preprints202604.0191.v1.

This excerpt provides direct evidence for remelting cold-pressed aluminum machining-chip briquettes, but not for loose aluminum powder, and it does not present a controlled powder-versus-swarf comparison. Sample B, produced from fragmented machining chips, generated a 2.25% dross fraction, 3.55% relative melting loss, and 94.2% metallurgical yield. Its remelted density was 2.388 g.cm⁻³, with residual porosity attributed to dissolved hydrogen, oxide-related effects, entrapped gases, and decomposed cutting oils or emulsions. The text identifies oxide layers on chips as Al₂O₃ sources that separate into dross and contribute to inclusions and metal burn-off; SEM–EDS measured 3.8–5.9 wt.% oxygen. Organic contamination reduced briquette density, released gas during heating, increased gas porosity and burn-off, and lowered yield. Remelting produced strong compositional homogenization: aluminum measured 97.21–97.51 wt.% across six XRF points, while iron varied from 0.38–0.63 wt.% because of randomly distributed inclusions; no significant Fe-, Mn-, or Si-enriched intermetallic segregation was detected by EDS. The excerpt gives no immersion or preheating protocol, melt time, melt temperature, stirring conditions, induction-power details, or fluxed-versus-flux-free comparison. It reports general industrial density targets of 2.20–2.40 g.cm⁻³ and yields of 90–96%, rather than experimental parameter-by-parameter comparisons.

## pqac-00000030

From text 'puga2009recyclingofaluminium pages 3-4'.

H. Puga, J. Barbosa, D. Soares, F. Silva, and S. Ribeiro. Recycling of aluminium swarf by direct incorporation in aluminium melts. Journal of Materials Processing Technology, 209:5195-5203, Jun 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2009.03.007, doi:10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2009.03.007. This article has 136 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides direct evidence for remelting machining aluminium swarf briquettes in an induction furnace, but not aluminium powder, and it does not report an explicit powder-versus-chip comparison or fluxed-versus-flux-free comparison. The study evaluated melting at 800, 850, 900, and 950 °C, with the melt held for 10 minutes after the last briquette; it also compared argon-protected and non-protected atmospheres. For treatment, the alloy was held at 850 °C for 10 minutes and then cooled to 730 °C for degassing, grain refinement, and silicon modification. Induction melting produced recovery rates of approximately 85%. The electromagnetic interaction generated stirring, which disrupted oxide films enclosing liquid aluminium and thereby increased recovered metal. In contrast, resistance melting was unsuitable: static melt behavior prevented oxide-envelope rupture, giving recovery below 60%, dross generation around 30%, and melting times approaching two hours. The excerpt does not state briquette immersion or preheating procedures, exact induction melt times, quantitative mixing uniformity, or final mechanical/physical properties. It does provide briquette moisture/density data: after pressure application, moisture was below 3 wt%, while densities at 300–500 bar were 2.03–2.10 kg/dm³.

## pqac-00000031

From text 'baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 9-11'.

Petr Baron, Jozef Mikita, and Vladimír Simkulet. Characterization of cold-pressed aluminum briquettes and their behavior during remelting for application in steel deoxidation. Unknown journal, Apr 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202604.0191.v1, doi:10.20944/preprints202604.0191.v1.

The excerpt provides direct evidence only for remelting cold-pressed briquettes made from recycled aluminum machining chips, not aluminum powder briquettes. Sample A is an Al–Si–Mg recycled-chip briquette compacted at 100–160 MPa and characterized for composition, density, porosity, and compaction. Its stated application is as an aluminum deoxidizing additive in steelmaking rather than specifically as feedstock for aluminum induction melting. Abstract:
AA7075 aluminum alloy is widely used for several high-technology applications for its high mechanical strength to weight ratio but is still the subject of several studies seeking a further increase in its mechanical properties. A commercial powder is used, either as-received or after ball-milling. Dense AA7075 samples are prepared in one step by Spark Plasma Sintering, at 550 °C with a holding time of 15 min and a uniaxial pressure of 100 MPa. No additional heat treatment is performed. Laser granulometry, X-ray diffraction and optical- and scanning electron microscopy show that both grain size and morphology are preserved in the dense samples, due to the relatively low temperature and short sintering time used. The samples prepared using the ball-milled powder exhibit both higher Vickers microhardness and transverse fracture strength values than those prepared using the raw powder, reflecting the finer microstructure.

Abstract:
In this study, the nano-aluminum powder was reinforced with a hybrid of copper and graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs). The ratios of GNPs were 0 wt%, 0.4 wt%, 0.6 wt%, 1.2 wt% and 1.8 wt%. To avoid the reaction between aluminum and graphene and, consequently, the formation of aluminum carbide, the GNP was first metalized with 5 wt% Ag and then coated with the predetermined 15 wt% Cu by the electroless coating process. In addition, the coating process was performed to improve the poor wettability between metal and ceramic. The Al/(GNPs-Ag)Cu nanocomposites with a high relative density of 99.9% were successfully prepared by the powder hot-pressing techniques. The effects of (GNPs/Ag) and Cu on the microstructure, density, hardness, and compressive strength of the Al-Cu nanocomposite were studied. As a result of agitating the GNPs during the cleaning and silver and Cu-plating, a homogeneous distribution was achieved. Some layers formed nano-tubes. The Al4C3 phase was not detected due to coating GNPs with Cu. The Cu9Al4 intermetallic was formed during the sintering process. The homogeneous dispersion of Cu and different ratios of GNs, good adhesion, and the formation of the new Cu9Al4 intermetallic improved in hardness. The pure aluminum sample recorded 216.2 HV, whereas Al/Cu reinforced with 1.8 GNs recorded 328.42 HV with a 51.9% increment. The compressive stress of graphene samples was improved upon increasing the GNPs contents. The Al-Cu/1.8 GNs sample recorded 266.99 MPa.

                  <jats:p>Metal matrix composites find applications across various scientific disciplines and are in high demand worldwide. Consequently, it is imperative to enhance their mechanical properties promptly. The manufacturing of metal matrix composites poses challenges when utilizing conventional methods due to issues such as agglomeration, interfacial reactions, and wetting difficulties. Thus, the most efficient approach for producing metal matrix nano-composites (MMNCs) is through powder metallurgy in conjunction with cold iso-static compaction. This technique offers the advantage of eliminating defects like nano-particle clustering and ensuring a uniform distribution of reinforcement particles within the matrix. The primary aim of this study is to evaluate previous research regarding the capability of powder metallurgy to utilize a cold iso-static compaction chamber for achieving a consistent distribution within the metal matrix.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Hot isostatic pressing (HIP) technology can directly produce nearly clean shaped workpieces that meet the requirements while ensuring machining accuracy and surface quality. Usually, people use numerical simulation methods to reduce experimental costs. Generally, a uniform powder relative density distribution of about 65% is used in the simulation. However, in practical engineering, we found that even with additional tools such as vibration tables, the powder filling is not uniform. The non-uniform distribution causes uneven shrinkage of the powder and capsule after HIP. In this paper, a numerical model for HIPing of Ti-6Al-4V powder is developed to improve the prediction by comparing the uniform and non-uniform initial powder distribution. The results show that different initial relative density distributions affect the powder densification process and further affect the deformation of the capsule. It also leads to non-uniform stress distribution after HIP, which increases the risk of capsule rupture. The analysis of the numerical simulation results and the comparison with the experimental results highlights that taking into account the non-uniform powder distribution inside the capsule is vital to improve numerical results and produce near-net shape components. The maximum error of the simulation with the usual initial relative density setting of 65% is 4.2%. However, considering the uneven distribution of initial powder, the maximum error is reduced to 3.16%, and the average error is also less than 2%.

Abstract:
This work provides an overview of the aluminum (Al) recycling process, from the scrap upgrading to the melting process. Innovations and new trends regarding the Al recycling technologies are highlighted. Aluminum recycling offers advantages in terms of environmental and economic benefits. The presence of deleterious impurities in recycled Al alloys is increasing and this is the main drawback if compared to primary alloys. The continuous growth of undesired elements can be mitigated by different technologies, preliminary operations and treatments, and by the optimization of the melting process. Downgrading and dilution are possible solutions to reduce the rate of impurities, but they are not sustainable if the final use of Al alloy continuously increases. The main objectives in the development of the Al recycling are shown and discussed. In particular, the evolution of preliminary treatments of the scrap, as sorting, comminution and de-coating, is reported and a review of the melting technologies is also presented. However, the choice of performing preliminary operations to the melting stage, thus improving the operating conditions during the furnace running, is a trade-off between costs and process efficiency.

                    Recent studies revealed that the addition of different grain refiner master alloys can affect the sedimentation and thus the spatial distribution of double oxide films in the melt. In this work, the interactions of TiB

The interactions between refiner particles and bifilms were studied by optical and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), while the changes in melt quality were analyzed by the computed tomographic (CT) analysis of reduced pressure test (RPT) specimens.                     <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>

                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>

                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    Ti particles. The attachment of grain refiner particles to double oxide films leads to the aided sedimentation of bifilms, which results in lowered porosity in RPT specimens. CFD simulations revealed that the experimentally observed fast sedimentation of TiB
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    can only be expected when relatively large particle agglomerates are created.

Abstract:
La presence d'inclusions dans les alliages d'aluminium est l'un des problemes les plus serieux rencontres lors du moulage de ces alliages. Les inclusions reduisent les proprietes mecaniques et augmentent la porosite; elles sont nuisibles a la finition de la surface et elles ont tendance a augmenter la corrosion. Quelques inclusions non metalliques fragiles agissent en tant que concentrations de contraintes et peuvent causer des bris prematures des composantes. Avec la demande croissante de pieces coulees en aluminium de plus haute qualite, particulierement dans les industries de l'automobile et de l'aerospatiale, beaucoup d'attention a ete pretee a la proprete du metal liquide. 
 
L'amelioration de la proprete de la fonte d'aluminium peut etre effectuee par des techniques d'enlevement ou par la surveillance des inclusions. Du point de vue de controle ou de surveillance, un certain nombre de techniques, telles que PoDFA (Porous Disc Filtration Analysis), LAIS (Liquid Aluminum Inclusion Sampler), Prefil (Pressure Filtration), et Qualiflash ont ete developpees pour mesurer les inclusions dans les fontes d'aluminium. Cependant, ces techniques prennent du temps et peuvent seulement fournir des resultats en dehors de la ligne de coulee; par consequent, l'information est souvent obtenue trop tard pour faire les ajustements necessaires dans le processus de coulee. Actuellement, bien qu'il y ait une technique de mesure en ligne disponible, a savoir LiMCA II, celle-ci est trop chere et par consequent n'est generalement pas accessible. 
 
La technique de detection a ultrasons semble etre une methode prometteuse pour resoudre le probleme des inclusions en raison de sa capacite a sonder l'interieur des materiaux. La presente etude a ete entreprise pour etudier la capacite de la technique ultrasonique pour mesurer diverses inclusions dans l'aluminium et dans l'alliage commercial de type 356 a deux temperatures differentes. 
 
Des inclusions de T1B2, d'AlSr, d'A^Ti, et d'A^C^ ont ete ajoutees aux alliages d'aluminium utilises pour etre etudiees a l'aide d'une machine "Metalvision MV20/20 ultrasonic". Les donnees obtenues ont fourni des informations sur (i) la valeur de proprete de Faluminium, (ii) la dimension moyenne des particules, et (iii) le nombre total de particules pour chaque gamme de dimension particulaire, en fonction du temps d'essai. Un examen de la microstructure des echantillons solidifies obtenus a partir des prelevements de la fonte a ete egalement effectue en utilisant une microsonde electronique de type Jeol JXA-8900L. 
 
La comparaison entre les resultats obtenus par la technique ultrasonique et les mesures effectuees par microsonde sur les microstructures correspondantes a montre que la machine ultrasomque peut etre utilisee comme dispositif en ligne pour determiner la proprete de la fonte pendant une longue periode (5 h dans la presente etude). Les courbes de proprete du metal liquide obtenues par la machine ultrasonique sont fiables et peuvent etre employees comme guide pour les coulees a condition que la temperature du bain liquide et les conditions d'agitation soient correctement ajustees. 
 
L'augmentation de la concentration des inclusions reduit le niveau de proprete de la fonte et est refletee par une diminution correspondante de la courbe de proprete de la fonte illustree par la machine ultrasonique, indiquant ainsi sa reponse relative au changement du niveau d'inclusions. L'augmentation de la temperature de coulee du metal liquide accelere cependant la decomposition de l'alliage mere, augmentant le nombre de particules d'inclusions dans la fonte et reduisant de ce fait la valeur de proprete de fonte. 
 
Normalement, quand les inclusions TiB2 sont ajoutees a la fonte d'aluminium, la fluidite de la fonte diminue de maniere significative. Les autres techniques d'analyse des inclusions (LiMCA et toutes les autres techniques de filtration) peuvent seulement detecter les inclusions T1B2 quand leur concentration est tres basse (moins de 10 ppm). En appliquant la technique a ultrasons, des mesures peuvent etre conduites correctement pour des concentrations aussi hautes que 90 ppm. Ceci indique que la technique ultrasomque fournit une alternative amelioree pour la mesure des mclusions TIB2 dans raluminium liquide. Ce fait est d'importance, puisque les mclusions sont invariablement presentes en raison de l'addition de TIB2 qui est essentielle aux processus d'affinage de grain utilises pour raluminium.

The best PM2324 microstructures from both methods had high sinter quality, no visible prior-particle boundaries, and only sporadic, isolated, rounded porosity. For PM7075, green density also increased with pressure and CIP was higher than die pressing; at 100 MPa, densities were only about 72–74%. The excerpt provides SPS data for pure Al and Al–0.4Mg powder, rather than conventional vacuum hot pressing or a direct argon-versus-vacuum comparison. Under 50 MPa applied pressure and a heating rate of 100 K min−1, density increased with sintering temperature, with pure Al requiring approximately 600°C for full densification and reaching up to 99.97% relative density. A 0.4% Mg addition disrupted the particle-surface oxide and enabled full densification at roughly 100°C lower temperature. Hold time and heating rate produced comparatively minor property gains, while applied pressure and temperature were the dominant variables. Increased thermal exposure caused microstructural coarsening and reduced hardness; oxide-rich prior-particle boundaries remained visible even after sintering at 600°C. Oxygen decreased substantially but remained detectable, with magnesium influencing the final oxygen level. It also describes electrostatic discharge as a plausible ignition source and recommends nitrogen purging/inerting to prevent flammable atmospheres in process equipment. For dryers, automated pressure-based interlocks, alarms, rotation shutdown, and nitrogen purge are suggested. The excerpt does not provide specific minimum ignition energy (MIE), minimum explosible concentration (MEC), or KST values specifically for 15–63 micron aluminum dust. It also does not address vacuum-pump-line filtration, metal-fire water-response procedures, personnel safety, or CIP pressure-vessel hazards in detail. This article has 38 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt provides published experimental information specifically for wet-bag cold isostatic pressing of pure iron powder, not a direct wet-bag versus dry-bag comparison. The apparatus was a wet-type CIP press using a thin-wall natural-rubber mold (1 mm thick) contained in a perforated aluminum fixture; the fixture was sealed with covers, bolts, and nuts for waterproofing, and air was evacuated from the mold before pressing. The mold was 40 mm high and 40 mm in diameter, while the alloy-steel mandrel was 40 mm high and 20 mm in diameter. Iron powder ASC 100.29, with an average particle size of 80 μm, was compacted around the mandrel to tap density. Smooth and coarse mandrels (reported roughness 0.8 S and 25 S) were used to study tooling friction. The paper’s central finding or subject is that powder–mandrel friction disturbs powder flow and produces density inhomogeneity, despite CIP’s usual advantage of homogeneous, isotropic microstructure. Mandrel friction coefficients were inferred from the relationship between compaction pressure and mandrel ejection pressure, and finite-element simulations using the Shima–Oyane constitutive model were compared with experiments. Abstract:
Al:Zr, Al-8Mg:Zr, and Al-38Mg:Zr nanocomposite particles fabricated by physical vapor deposition (PVD) and ball milling were reacted in 1 atm of pure O2 within a custom, highly-sensitive micro-bomb calorimeter. The heats of combustion were compared to examine the effect of particle size and composition on combustion efficiency under room temperature and in a fixed volume. All particles yielded ~60–70% of their theoretical maximum heat of combustion and exhibited an increase in heat over composite thin films of similar compositions, which is attributed to an increase in the surface area to volume ratio. The effect of particle size and geometry are mitigated owing to the sintering of the particles within the crucible, implying the importance of particle dispersion for enhanced performance. Vaporization of the metal species may transition between two diffusion flame species (Mg to Al). As Mg content is increased, more vaporization may occur at lower temperatures, leading to an additional stage of sintering. Physically intermixed Al and Mg oxides have been observed coating the surface of the particles, which implies a continuous transition of these vaporization processes. Such nano-oxides imply high vapor-flame combustion temperatures (>2700 K) and suggest viability for agent defeat applications.

Abstract:
The connective hard tissues bone and teeth are highly porous on a micrometer scale, but show high values of compression strength at a relatively low weight. The fabrication of porous materials has been actively researched and different processes have been developed that vary in preparation complexity and also in the type of porous material that they produce. Methodologies are available for determination of pore properties. The purpose of the paper is to give an overview of these methods, the role of porosity in natural porous materials and the effect of pore properties on the living tissues. The minimum pore size required to allow the ingrowth of mineralized tissue seems to be in the order of 50 µm: larger pore sizes seem to improve speed and depth of penetration of mineralized tissues into the biomaterial, but on the other hand impair the mechanical properties. The optimal pore size is therefore dependent on the application and the used material.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    In this work, Porous copper foam samples were fabricated by a space-holder technique with water-atomized copper powder and sodium chloride (NaCl) particles in weight fractions ranging from 10 to 35 wt%. The powders were mechanically mixed at a 10:1 ball-to-powder ratio and 150 rpm for 2 h. The effects of space-holder content on the physical, mechanical, tribological, and electrochemical performance were systematically investigated. Increasing the NaCl fraction precisely controlled the total porosity, from 39.15% to 57.76%, and reduced the bulk density from 5.452 to 3.785 g/cm³. XRD and SEM analyses confirmed a single-phase FCC copper matrix and a structural transition from isolated pores to a highly interconnected open-cell network. Consequently, Vickers hardness, compressive yield strength, energy absorption capacity decreased from 52.12 to 29.23 HV, 18.25 to 1.65 MPa, and 35.73 to 10.46 MJ/m³, respectively, following a modified Gibson–Ashby model (R
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                     = 0.95). Concurrently, the coefficient of friction and specific wear rate increased (reaching a maximum of 0.73 mm³/N·m under 15 N for 35 wt% NaCl) due to strut thinning and localized delamination. Electrochemical evaluation in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution revealed an optimization threshold for sample fabricated with 25 wt% NaCl, which exhibited the lowest corrosion rate of 0.918 mm/y, and the highest polarization resistance (Rp) of 267.28 Ω, due to a stable Cu
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O passive film. Exceeding this threshold at 30 and 35 wt% NaCl led to structural instability and stagnant electrolyte zones, accelerating corrosion kinetics. Overall, lower-porosity porous copper foam architectures offer superior structural energy absorption, whereas the 25 wt% NaCl configuration achieves an optimal balance between mechanical integrity and corrosion resistance.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
The cover systems in contaminated sites have some problems, including desiccation cracks, which would lead to degradation of the barrier performance. This study presented a systemic laboratory experimental investigation on the liquid–plastic limit, moisture retention, hydraulic conductivity (k), and gas diffusion barrier properties of amended compacted clay by attapulgite and diatomite for controlling desiccation cracks and migration of water and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). The results showed that the attapulgite could enhance the moisture retention and liquid limit of amended compacted clay. Diatomite could reduce the gas diffusion coefficient (Dθ) significantly. The compacted clay amended by the dual-additives component of attapulgite and diatomite could enhance the liquid limit, moisture retention percent, gas barrier property, and hydraulic performance compared with the unamended clay. Based on the experimental data obtained, the dosage of additives was targeted to be 5%. The moisture retention percent of dual-additives (attapulgite 4% and diatomite 1%) amended clay increased by 82%, the k decreased by 25%, and the Dθ decreased by 42% compared with unamended clay. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM), BET-specific surface area test method (BET), Mercury Intrusion Porosimetry (MIP), and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) indicated the enhancement mechanism of additives-amended compacted clay.

The excerpt provides directly relevant thermal-explosion/SHS information only for Ti–Al powder compacts, not for Al–Ni, Fe–Al, or Al–Zr, and it contains no evidence about low-concentration alloying additions in excess aluminium. Four Ti–Al compositions were examined, corresponding to Al3Ti, AlTi, AlTi + AlTi3, and AlTi3, so the reported behavior includes both near-stoichiometric intermetallic compositions and a two-phase composition. For Ti–40 wt% Al (TiAl), two exothermic events occurred. The first ignited at approximately 550 °C, with the broader first-peak ignition range reported as 520–570 °C; this ignition temperature was essentially insensitive to heating rate. The second event is associated with aluminium melting and liquid Al reacting with solid Ti: at heating rates of 10 K min−1 or less, ignition occurs near aluminium’s melting point (about 660 °C). At higher heating rate, ignition shifts lower; at 50 K min−1 it begins below the Al melting point, indicating a possible solid Al–solid Ti reaction contribution. Thus, the approximately 500–570 °C ignition applies to the first Ti–Al exotherm, while the second ignition is near 660 °C at low heating rate and can fall below 660 °C at high heating rate. The excerpt provides useful process data for remelting aluminium swarf briquettes, although it does not directly address mixtures of Al powder with Si, Cu, Mg, Mn, Fe, Ni, Ti, or Zr, nor does it report pure-powder solubility limits or intermetallic formation. In an induction furnace, an argon atmosphere increased average aluminium recovery from 60.8% to 83.3% by reducing oxidation and dross generation. Briquette density strongly affected melting: lower compaction pressure produced higher recovery, while increased pressure reduced porosity, hindered molten-metal penetration, lengthened melting time, and increased dross. Briquettes compacted at 300 bar performed better than those compacted at 400–500 bar; the reported 300-bar trials produced approximately 88.2–91.3% recovery, compared with roughly 75.0–78.3% at 500 bar. Initial molten-pool size also mattered: pools above 33.3% of the charge achieved approximately 90% recovery, whereas around 20% reduced recovery to about 85% or lower, likely because briquettes contacted the atmosphere and oxidized. The selected conditions were approximately 15 kg charge, 33.3% initial molten pool, 66.7% briquettes, 300-bar compaction, 850 °C, argon, and 60 minutes.

The excerpt provides only limited information relevant to comparing CIP and uniaxial compaction. It states that PM2324 and PM7075 produced broadly comparable sintered quality by either method, but PM2324 responded differently to pressure: lower pressures were preferred for CIP, while higher pressures improved products made by die compaction. CIP was identified as advantageous for producing uniform green density and for compacting larger parts. The experiments used the same nominal pressure range, 100–400 MPa, for both methods, although the specimens had different geometries and the CIP compacts were cylindrical rubber-moulded bodies. The excerpt does not report pressure-depressurization rates, green strength measurements, direct evidence of particle-oxide-film fragmentation, or comparisons with the cited studies by Andasmas (2011) and Wei (2011). It therefore cannot establish whether oxide rupture during CIP is better or worse than during uniaxial compaction at the same density. Also, identical nominal pressure or density does not by itself demonstrate equivalent oxide disruption, since pressure path, friction, stress state, particle rearrangement, and unloading history may differ.

From text 'chua2014developmentofaluminumd pages 31-34'.

The excerpt provides qualitative and practical guidance on pore connectivity during heating, but it does not report a measured sharp pore-closure threshold for pure aluminum compacts at 85–90% bulk density, nor does it present quantitative gas-release measurements up to 500 °C. Its key distinction is between total density/porosity and whether pores remain interconnected: vacuum degassing depends on interconnected pores so that released gases can escape. The text states that approximately 75% of theoretical green density is a typical upper limit for achieving appropriate degassing, implying that higher compaction may restrict gas transport as pores become less connected. However, this is described as a typical processing limit rather than a universal, experimentally identified transition or critical density. The excerpt also explains that residual pores can remain after sintering and act as stress concentrators, while oxide networks may impair ductility and fatigue resistance. info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully

Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:

Use the tools to answer the question: We make small batches of aluminium-alloy powder by ultrasonic atomization (AMAZEMET rePOWDER, induction-heated module). We are deciding how to turn **pure aluminium powder** (gas-atomized, roughly 15-63 µm, alone or blended with alloying-element or master-alloy powders) into **green parts** that we then melt in the atomizer crucible together with solid alloy (6063 rod, 4047). We want a **pros-and-cons comparison of two consolidation routes**, (A) powder-metallurgy pressing under vacuum and (B) cold isostatic pressing (CIP), judged on **safety** first, then simplicity, speed, cost, and whether the green part will melt, coalesce and mix into the rest of the melt. Please answer from the literature, with citations (DOIs where possible), give numbers wherever the sources have them, and say explicitly which conclusions come from direct evidence for aluminium and which are extrapolated from other metals or from general PM practice.

**Set-up.** Graphite crucible (BN-coated), induction heated, 10-11 cm deep, with a sealing (stopper) rod down the middle; the melt is bottom-poured through a ~0.7 mm hBN nozzle onto a 40 kHz vibrating molybdenum plate. The charge is loaded cold. The chamber is then evacuated and back-filled with argon several times ("gas washes"), including while the charge is held at about 500 °C and still solid. It is then melted under argon at about 0.2 bar overpressure (13-20 ppm O2), set point 810-840 °C, held about 2 minutes (we may extend this to 5-10 minutes), with no mechanical stirring beyond the induction field. Charges are 170-350 g. Every piece must be under 20 mm across to fit between the stopper rod and the crucible wall, so a green part would be a slug about 19 mm in diameter and 20-60 mm long (roughly 10-40 g).

**What we already know** (our own runs, and an earlier literature review on 2026-11-02 that you do not need to repeat). Loose gas-atomized powder sealed in a 6063 cup did not consolidate in one run (AlSi10Mg) and did in another (4047); the oxide shell on each particle, plus MgO or spinel when Mg is present, keeps the molten droplets apart. Cold uniaxial pressing of Al powder reaches about 85 % relative density at about 100 MPa and 92-98 % at 250-580 MPa; it cracks the oxide but does not remove it. Pores start to close above roughly 85-90 % density, so a denser compact can seal in air, adsorbed water and water from hydrated oxide. The equipment maker warned that powder compressed inside a closed aluminium cup could eject molten metal, presumably from trapped gas. Die lubricants add gas and carbon. Cast master alloys, or an arc-melted button made from the weighed powders, were ranked above any pressed compact.

**The two routes to compare.**
- **(A) "Powder metallurgy under vacuum":** uniaxial die pressing with the die cavity evacuated before and during pressing (an evacuable die with a vacuum port and O-ring seals, or a die inside a vacuum chamber or glovebox), with or without vacuum drying or degassing of the loose powder beforehand. Please also cover the natural extensions: pressing followed by vacuum sintering or degassing, and vacuum hot pressing (for example 300-550 °C).
- **(B) Cold isostatic pressing (CIP):** powder filled into a flexible elastomer mould (polyurethane, latex, silicone or rubber bag), optionally evacuated and sealed, and pressed hydrostatically (typically 100-400 MPa) by a water-based fluid or oil. Wet-bag versus dry-bag; buying a small laboratory CIP versus sending parts to a toll-pressing service. Also the combination of A and B: powder vacuum-degassed first, sealed in an evacuated bag, then cold isostatically pressed.

**Please address:**

1. **Pros and cons of each route (and its sub-variants) for pure aluminium powder**, ideally as a table covering: process safety; safety of the green part when melted in our crucible; green density achievable versus pressure, and its uniformity (density gradients and low-density zones in uniaxially pressed slugs with height-to-diameter ratios of about 1-3, versus isostatic pressing); green strength, edge integrity and powder shedding during handling; the need for lubricants and their effect; contamination (lubricant residue, bag material, pressing fluid, die wear); dimensional control (our 20 mm limit, CIP shrinkage and shape tolerance); oxide-film disruption (does hydrostatic loading in CIP break the particle oxide films more or less than the shear in a uniaxial die?); residual gas and moisture in the part; simplicity and the skill needed; time per part and per batch; and cost (equipment capital, tooling and consumables, and toll-service pricing if published).
2. **Which route makes the safer green part to melt in the atomizer, and why.** Quantify where possible: adsorbed and chemically bound water on gas-atomized Al powder (mass %, or mL H2 per 100 g Al) and the temperatures at which it is released; the open-to-closed porosity transition for Al compacts; how much evacuating the die or the CIP bag before pressing reduces the trapped gas; and whether an open-pore green compact heated slowly through our vacuum and argon washes up to about 500 °C would degas in place before its pores close. What are the failure modes: a CIP bag leak or puncture that lets water or oil into the powder (and the hydrogen that water generates with freshly exposed Al), lubricant decomposition, trapped air expanding on heating, lamination or end-capping cracks from uniaxial pressing?
3. **Process hazards of each route** when handling fine pure Al powder: combustible-dust and ignition risks while filling dies or bags, drawing fine powder into a vacuum line or pump, venting an evacuated die to air, contact with the CIP fluid, stored energy in the high-pressure vessel, and safe practice for each (inert handling, filters, grounding, PPE).
4. **Melt-in and mixing feasibility.** Would a green part from either route (at what density) melt, coalesce and mix into a 6063 melt at 810-840 °C under argon within 2-10 minutes with only induction stirring? Does CIP versus uniaxial pressing versus vacuum hot pressing change coalescence, metal yield, dross or oxide inclusions on remelting? Use evidence from remelting Al powder compacts, chip or swarf briquettes, PM parts and foundry alloying tablets. If alloying powders (Si, Cu, Mg, Mn, Fe, Ni, Ti, Zr) are blended into the pure Al before pressing: segregation while filling, and exothermic reactions between Al and these powders on heating (for example the self-propagating Al-Ni, Al-Ti, Al-Fe or Al-Zr reactions in pressed compacts, and how compact density affects ignition), and whether these help or hurt safety and dissolution.
5. **A practical recipe for each route** for a 19 mm diameter by 20-60 mm slug: pressure, dwell, evacuation level, drying or degassing temperature and time, lubricant (or none), mould or die material and sizing, expected density, and how to check a part before it goes into the crucible (Archimedes density and open porosity, a weight-loss or gas-release test on heating). What press force, or what CIP vessel size and pressure rating, does this need?
6. **Recommendation:** which route, or neither, would you choose for a university lab making a few such parts per week, and when would each be the wrong choice? Compare briefly with buying cast master alloys or arc-melting a button from the weighed powders.

Abstract:
Abstract Metals and alloys are among the most technologically important materials for our industrialized societies. They are the most common structural materials used in cars, airplanes and buildings, and constitute the technological core of most electronic devices. They allow the transportation of energy over great distances and are exploited in critical parts of renewable energy technologies. Even though primary metal production industries are mature and operate optimized pyrometallurgical processes, they extensively rely on cheap and abundant carbonaceous reactants (fossil fuels, coke), require high power heating units (which are also typically powered by fossil fuels) to calcine, roast, smelt and refine, and they generate many output streams with high residual energy content. Many unit operations also generate hazardous gaseous species on top of large CO_2 emissions which require gas-scrubbing and capture strategies for the future. Therefore, there are still many opportunities to lower the environmental footprint of key pyrometallurgical operations. This paper explores the possibility to use greener reactants such as bio-fuels, bio-char, hydrogen and ammonia in different pyrometallurgical units. It also identifies all recycled streams that are available (such as steel and aluminum scraps, electronic waste and Li-ion batteries) as well as the technological challenges associated with their integration in primary metal processes. A complete discussion about the alternatives to carbon-based reduction is constructed around the use of hydrogen, metallo-reduction as well as inert anode electrometallurgy. The review work is completed with an overview of the different approaches to use renewable energies and valorize residual heat in pyrometallurgical units. Finally, strategies to mitigate environmental impacts of pyrometallurgical operations such as CO_2 capture utilization and storage as well as gas scrubbing technologies are detailed. This original review paper brings together for the first time all potential strategies and efforts that could be deployed in the future to decrease the environmental footprint of the pyrometallurgical industry. It is primarily intended to favour collaborative work and establish synergies between academia, the pyrometallurgical industry, decision-makers and equipment providers. Graphical abstract Highlights A more sustainable production of metals using greener reactants, green electricity or carbon capture is possible and sometimes already underway. More investments and pressure are required to hasten change. Discussion Is there enough pressure on the aluminum and steel industries to meet the set climate targets? The greenhouse gas emissions of existing facilities can often be partly mitigated by retrofitting them with green technologies, should we close plants prematurely to build new plants using greener technologies? Since green or renewable resources presently have limited availability, in which sector should we use them to maximize their benefits?

Abstract:
This overview paper describes the interaction of powder metallurgical iron-base alloys with the atmosphere during sintering. The methods of thermal analysis serve to clarify the processes that take place especially during the heating stage of the sintering cycle. After a discussion of the physical and chemical fundamentals of the sintering process, the methods of thermal analysis are explained. The differences between plain iron and alloyed systems are discussed in detail. Classical PM low alloy steels with alloying elements, such as Cu, Ni and Mo, react in a similar way as unalloyed carbon steels. The situation changes dramatically, when oxygen sensitive elements as chromium, manganese and even more silicon come into play. The removal of the surface oxygen is much more crucial, and there are several competing reactions, which have to be considered when these systems should be sintered in industrial scale to reach the desired mechanical and dimensional properties.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study presents a comprehensive characterization of recycled aluminum briquettes produced by cold pressing of Al–Si–Mg alloy machining chips, along with an evaluation of their behavior during subsequent remelting. The objective was to assess the density, porosity, chemical composition, and metallurgical yield of the briquettes before and after melting, as well as to determine their suitability for use as deoxidizing additives in steelmaking. The cold-pressed briquette (Sample A) exhibited a low density of 2.29 g.cm-³ and a porosity of 12.1%, resulting from intergranular voids and residual lubricants. After melting and resolidification (Sample B), the density increased to 2.388 g.cm-3 and the porosity decreased to 8.15%. XRF chemical analysis confirmed a high degree of elemental homogeneity after melting with no indication of segregation, while SEM–EDS microstructural analysis verified the absence of significant intermetallic phases and revealed only a thin surface oxide layer. The metallurgical yield reached 94.2% with a low dross content (2.25%). The results demonstrate that, following appropriate preprocessing and optimized compaction, recycled aluminum briquettes constitute a stable and efficient secondary aluminum material suitable for steel deoxidation, and they can significantly reduce the environmental impact of metallurgical production.</jats:p>

Abstract:

 This critical review examines advances in preprocessing and remelting processes for aluminium alloy chip recycling, emphasizing pre-treatment and remelting techniques that improve both resource recovery and material quality. Pre-treatment strategies, particularly cleaning methods and compaction are critically evaluated. Various cleaning methods, including centrifugation, ultrasonic solvent washing, extraction, and distillation are compared based on their ability to remove residual cutting fluids. Cold compaction, which augments chip density to approximately 2.5 g/cm³, significantly curtails oxidation losses and enhances metal recovery. During remelting, NaCl-KCl-based fluxes with limited fluoride additions (e.g., 3–7 wt% Na₃AlF₆) disrupt oxide networks but require careful dosage control to minimize furnace corrosion and environmental hazards. Moreover, mechanical stirring combined with suitable melting temperatures reduces porosity while enhancing melt purity. Future research should prioritize the development of low-energy cleaning methods, flux composition optimization, and scalable production techniques to further advance sustainable aluminium recycling.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Aluminum recycling is pivotal for achieving carbon neutrality and advancing the circular economy, offering significant reductions in energy use and greenhouse gas emissions compared to primary production. This review synthesizes global advances from 2020 to 2025 in scrap collection, sorting, remelting, and alloy recovery, with a focus on technological progress, sustainability metrics, and policy integration. Secondary aluminum already supplies over one-third of global demand and could surpass 50 % by 2030 with stronger segregation systems and extended producer responsibility (EPR) schemes. Innovations such as high-shear degassing, solid-state chip recycling, and chloride-free refining have improved melt quality and reduced salt-slag waste. At the same time, life-cycle assessments indicate up to 95% lower emissions compared to virgin aluminum. Persistent barriers remain—namely alloy contamination, inconsistent scrap classification, and limited traceability in informal collection networks. Regional policy experiences demonstrate that harmonized standards, mandatory recycled-content targets, and digital traceability accelerate market adaptation, whereas developing economies still face fragmented logistics and weak governance. Future directions include integrating real-time life-cycle assessment, artificial intelligence-based scrap sorting, and international alloy standards, enabling over 80% recycled content. Overall, aluminum recycling emerges as a technologically mature, economically competitive, and environmentally decisive route for decarbonizing metallurgical production and supporting the global energy transition.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Rotary furnaces remain important in secondary aluminum production because they can process oxidized, coated, low-density, contaminated, and dross-rich feeds that are difficult to recover in conventional bath furnaces. Their flexibility creates a recovery–residue trade-off: heat, rotation, and chloride–fluoride fluxes can liberate and coalesce metal droplets, but may also increase oxidation, emissions, refractory attack, and salt-slag generation. This structured critical narrative review evaluates a coded corpus of 106 publications from 2020 to August 2026. Retrospective A–E classification was performed by one reviewer and represents interpretive judgments of industrial transferability. No level-A repeated industrial campaign with closed aluminum–salt–energy–quality balances was identified. Accordingly, the proposed nine-gate Feedstock–Flux–Furnace–Residue framework is a testable decision architecture rather than a validated control model; low-salt and salt-free strategies remain feed-specific and require prospective industrial validation.</jats:p>
