Abstract:
Ceramic matrix composites reinforced with carbon nanotubes are becoming increasingly popular in industry due to their astonishing mechanical properties and taking into account the fact that advanced production technologies make carbon nanotubes increasingly affordable. In the present paper, the most convenient contemporary methods used for the compaction of molding masses composed of either technical ceramics or ceramic matrix composites reinforced with carbon nanotubes are surveyed. This stage that precedes debinding and sintering plays the key role in getting pore-free equal-density ceramics at the scale of mass production. The methods include: compaction in sealed and collector molds, cold isostatic and quasi-isostatic compaction; dynamic compaction methods, such as magnetic pulse, vibration, and ultrasonic compaction; extrusion, stamping, and injection; casting from aqueous and non-aqueous slips; tape and gel casting. Capabilities of mold-free approaches to produce precisely shaped ceramic bodies are also critically analyzed, including green ceramic machining and additive manufacturing technologies.

Abstract:
We provide a systematic overview of the mechanochemical reactions of inorganic solids, notably simple binary compounds, such as oxides, nitrides, carbides, sulphides, phosphides, hydrides, borides, borane derivatives, and related systems. Whereas the solid state has been traditionally considered to be of little synthetic value by the broader community of synthetic chemists, the solid-state community, and in particular researchers focusing on the reactions of inorganic materials, have thrived in building a rich and dynamic research field based on mechanically-driven transformations of inorganic substances typically seen as inert and high-melting. This review provides an insight into the chemical richness of such mechanochemical reactions and, at the same time, offers their tentative categorisation based on transformation type, resulting in seven distinct groupings: (i) the formation of adducts, (ii) the reactions of dehydration; (iii) oxidation–reduction (redox) reactions; (iv) metathesis (or exchange) reactions; (v) doping and structural rearrangements, including reactions involving the reaction vessel (the milling jar); (vi) acid–base reactions, and (vii) other, mixed type reactions. At the same time, we offer a parallel description of inorganic mechanochemical reactions depending on the reaction conditions, as those that: (i) take place under mild conditions (e.g., manual grinding using a mortar and a pestle); (ii) proceed gradually under mechanical milling; (iii) are self-sustained and initiated by mechanical milling, i.e., mechanically induced self-propagating reactions (MSRs); and (iv) proceed only via harsh grinding and are a result of chemical reactivity under strongly non-equilibrium conditions. By elaborating on typical examples and general principles in the mechanochemistry of hard and high-melting substances, this review provides a suitable complement to the existing literature, focusing on the properties and mechanochemical reactions of inorganic solids, such as nanomaterials and catalysts.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Metal powders have both a high specific energy and a high energy density, which explains their widespread use in energetic materials (propellants, explosives and pyrotechnics). Pyrotechnic compositions are used extensively for both civilian and military applications. However, the combustion of pyrotechnics remains challenging to understand or predict due to the diversity of the components and the wide range of parameters that affect their results. Therefore, ongoing research efforts worldwide aim to investigate the combustion mechanisms of pyrotechnic compositions to improve their performance. In this review, studies on the ignition and combustion mechanisms of four metal powders (Al, Mg, Fe and B) are discussed. Moreover, their use as fuel in pyrotechnic systems is reported, as well as the combustion performance and energy release of the pyrotechnic mixtures. Additionally, some mixtures composed of fluorinated oxidizers and Al, Mg and B are also presented. Thermal analysis methods such as DSC and TG are used to obtain the thermal behavior of the pyrotechnic compositions. Furthermore, parameters such as particle size and the equivalence ratio that affect the performance of pyrotechnic mixtures and those that remain little studied are reported in this review.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000000

From text 'yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 2-4'.

Michiaki Yamasaki and Yoshihito Kawamura. Changes in the surface characteristics of gas-atomized pure aluminum powder during vacuum degassing. Materials Transactions, 47:1902-1905, Aug 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.2320/matertrans.47.1902, doi:10.2320/matertrans.47.1902. This article has 29 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Yamasaki and Kawamura directly measured water adsorption, temperature-programmed desorption (TPD), and XPS changes during vacuum degassing of gas-atomized pure aluminum powder (Materials Transactions 47, 1902–1905, 2006; DOI: 10.2320/matertrans.47.1902). The H2O-derived BET surface area was 0.125 m² g−1, and the adsorption isotherm showed a low-pressure hysteresis loop, interpreted as ultramicropores in the surface layer. Humid-air-exposed powder released H2O beginning near 480 K, with a peak near 720 K; H2O desorption was not detected after exposure to dry air or high-purity argon. Hydrogen evolution increased sharply at approximately 620 and 660 K and peaked at approximately 725 K, while no low-temperature H2 evolution was observed around 473 K. XPS indicated increasing dehydration and crystallization with temperature, with amorphous hydrated alumina transforming to crystalline α-Al2O3 at about 623 K. The authors distinguish this oxide transformation from later hydrogen release: oxidation of aluminum by hydration water produces chemisorbed surface hydrogen at 623 K, followed by recombination/desorption as H2 around 725 K. The excerpt does not provide numerical hydrogen volumes, absolute vacuum pressure, pore-closure measurements, or CIP-versus-die-pressing data.


---

## pqac-00000001

From text 'yamasaki2006changesinthe pages 1-2'.

Michiaki Yamasaki and Yoshihito Kawamura. Changes in the surface characteristics of gas-atomized pure aluminum powder during vacuum degassing. Materials Transactions, 47:1902-1905, Aug 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.2320/matertrans.47.1902, doi:10.2320/matertrans.47.1902. This article has 29 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Yamasaki and Kawamura directly examined 99.99% rapidly solidified, gas-atomized pure Al powder with a mean particle diameter of approximately 25 µm. For temperature-programmed desorption (TPD), powders were exposed for 24 hours at room temperature to humid air (>40% moisture), dry air (<20 ppm moisture), or high-purity argon (<0.5 ppm oxygen and moisture), then heated at 5 K min−1 under 10−3 Pa vacuum while desorbed gases were analyzed by quadrupole mass spectrometry. The reported H2O adsorption-derived BET surface area was 0.125 m2 g−1. Hydrated-Al2O3 decomposition to crystalline Al2O3 occurred at 623 K, whereas hydrogen desorption occurred at 725 K, indicating separate reactions. In humid-air-exposed powder, H2 desorption increased sharply at approximately 620–660 K and peaked at 725 K; no H2 desorption was detected after dry-air or high-purity-argon exposure. The excerpt does not provide quantitative adsorbed-water volumes, total hydrogen volumes, pore-closure measurements, trapped-gas data, CIP versus die-pressing density, oxide strength, or compaction uniformity, nor does it contain the Chua (2014) or Wei (2011) studies. The article DOI is 10.2320/matertrans.47.1902.

## pqac-00000002

From text 'wei2011fulldensityconsolidation pages 2-4'.

Xian-shun Wei, B. Vekshin, V. Kraposhin, Yong-jiang Huang, J. Shen, and K. Xia. Full density consolidation of pure aluminium powders by cold hydro-mechanical pressing. Materials Science and Engineering A-structural Materials Properties Microstructure and Processing, 528:5784-5789, Jul 2011. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.msea.2011.03.099, doi:10.1016/j.msea.2011.03.099. This article has 22 citations.

The excerpt provides direct quantitative experiments for gas-atomized commercial pure aluminium powder using cold hydro-mechanical pressing (CHMP), not Yamasaki’s water/hydroxide-degassing study or a direct CIP-versus-die-pressure comparison. The powder had particle sizes of 20–140 μm, with a 57 μm average. It was sealed in a rubber bag without degassing. CHMP applied axial compression together with radial pressure; the radial pressure was described as approximately 1 GPa, while one reported lower-pressure configuration used 300 MPa radial pressure. Two compact conditions achieved relative densities of 99.3% (C1) and 99.9% (C2). C2 had greater hardness than C1, 49.7 versus 44.5 (micro-Vickers values). Reported yield strengths were 118.5 MPa for C1 and 158.7 MPa for C2, compared with 87.6 MPa for as-cast high-purity aluminium. EBSD gave average grain sizes of 5 μm for C1 and 1 μm for C2; TEM estimated C2 at 0.5–1.5 μm. TEM/HRTEM found amorphous Al2O3 layers at particle boundaries. The excerpt does not give adsorbed-water quantities, hydroxide decomposition, hydrogen volumes versus temperature or vacuum, explicit pore-closure measurements, trapped-gas pressure/volume, or a CIP/die-pressure comparison. DOI: 10.1016/j.msea.2011.03.099.

## pqac-00000003

From text 'sweet2014advancedsinteringtechniquesa pages 61-65'.

G Sweet. Advanced sintering techniques of aluminum: spark plasma sintering. Unknown journal, 2014.

The excerpt provides quantitative SPS degassing observations for aluminum and Al–0.4Mg powders, but it does not contain the requested direct Yamasaki (2006), Chua (2014), or Wei (2011) experiments, nor any DOI information. Under vacuum, moderate temperatures promote decomposition of hydrated surface phases, with degassing typically lasting hours. Physisorbed water is released below approximately 175°C; chemisorbed hydroxide/water-containing phases decompose over approximately 150–550°C. Hydrogen evolution begins above 200°C and peaks near 450°C. The cited reactions are aluminum hydrate decomposition to alumina and water, followed by aluminum/water reaction producing alumina and hydrogen; analogous magnesium reactions are also given. For SPS samples, initial oxygen contents were approximately 3000 ppm for Al and 1730 ppm for Al–0.4Mg, while initial hydrogen contents were approximately 69 and 54 ppm, respectively. Measured net oxygen-to-hydrogen loss ratios were 16:1–20:1 for Al and 16:1–27:1 for Al–0.4Mg, indicating excess oxygen release relative to the expected 8:1 water-loss ratio. In size-effect experiments, 20 mm specimens exceeded 99% relative density across the studied temperatures, whereas larger 80 mm slugs required higher temperatures. At 400°C residual gases increased; at temperatures ≥500°C both oxygen and hydrogen were substantially reduced. The passage discusses residual porosity and possible rehydration after vacuum removal, but does not quantify pore closure or trapped-gas volumes.

## pqac-00000004

From text 'chua2014developmentofaluminuma pages 95-98'.

AS Chua. Development of aluminum powder metallurgy alloys for aerospace applications. Unknown journal, 2014.

This excerpt provides quantitative results for spark plasma sintering (SPS) of PM2024 and PM7075 aluminum alloy powders, not gas-atomized pure aluminum. At a 400°C peak temperature, SPS samples reached greater than 99.5% theoretical density. In the T6 temper, reported apparent hardness values were 71 HRB for PM2024 and 87 HRB for PM7075. SPS produced substantial reductions in residual oxygen and hydrogen, with evolved-gas analysis attributing the reductions principally to release of CO2 and adsorbed/chemisorbed H2O. Trace oxygen was also consumed by temperature-dependent self-gettering at particle surfaces, partially reversing oxygen removal; the excerpt states that this gettering response was broadly consistent between the powders. Particle size affected processing: particles with nominal size at least 180 µm gave enhanced densification and minimized O/H impurities. Figure 4.15 compares oxygen loss for 180 µm and 45 µm particles in both alloys, but the excerpt does not provide numerical oxygen-loss values. It contains no Yamasaki 2006 data on pure aluminum hydroxide decomposition, hydrogen volumes, vacuum degassing, or temperature-specific gas evolution; no CIP-versus-die-pressure comparison; no trapped-gas or pore-closure measurements; and no DOI. The cited information therefore supports only limited Chua 2014 SPS density, hardness, gas-release, and particle-size context.

Bimetals—materials composed of two metal components with dissimilar standard reduction–oxidation (redox) potentials—offer unique electronic, optical, and catalytic properties, surpassing monometallic systems. These materials exhibit not only the combined attributes of their constituent metals but also new and novel properties arising from their synergy. Although many reviews have explored the synthesis, properties, and applications of bimetallic systems, none have focused exclusively on iron (Fe)- and aluminum (Al)-based bimetals. This systematic review addresses this gap by providing a comprehensive overview of conventional and emerging techniques for Fe-based and Al-based bimetal synthesis. Specifically, this work systematically reviewed recent studies from 2014 to 2023 using the Scopus, Web of Science (WoS), and Google Scholar databases, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, and was registered under INPLASY with the registration number INPLASY202540026. Articles were excluded if they were inaccessible, non-English, review articles, conference papers, book chapters, or not directly related to the synthesis of Fe- or Al-based bimetals. Additionally, a bibliometric analysis was performed to evaluate the research trends on the synthesis of Fe-based and Al-based bimetals. Based on the 122 articles analyzed, Fe-based and Al-based bimetal synthesis methods were classified into three types: (i) physical, (ii) chemical, and (iii) biological techniques. Physical methods include mechanical alloying, radiolysis, sonochemical methods, the electrical explosion of metal wires, and magnetic field-assisted laser ablation in liquid (MF-LAL). In comparison, chemical protocols covered reduction, dealloying, supported particle methods, thermogravimetric methods, seed-mediated growth, galvanic replacement, and electrochemical synthesis. Meanwhile, biological techniques utilized plant extracts, chitosan, alginate, and cellulose-based materials as reducing agents and stabilizers during bimetal synthesis. Research works on the synthesis of Fe-based and Al-based bimetals initially declined but increased in 2018, followed by a stable trend, with 50% of the total studies conducted in the last five years. China led in the number of publications (62.3%), followed by Russia, Australia, and India, while Saudi Arabia had the highest number of citations per document (95). RSC Advances was the most active journal, publishing eight papers from 2014 to 2023, while Applied Catalysis B: Environmental had the highest number of citations per document at 203. Among the three synthesis methods, chemical techniques dominated, particularly supported particles, galvanic replacement, and chemical reduction, while biological and physical methods have started gaining interest. Iron–copper (Fe/Cu), iron–aluminum (Fe/Al), and iron–nickel (Fe/Ni) were the most commonly synthesized bimetals in the last 10 years. Finally, this work was funded by DOST-PCIEERD and DOST-ERDT.

## 2. Mechanical characterization of high volume fraction Al7075-Al_2O_3 composite fabricated by semisolid powder processing
Valid Text Names:

    author = "Aghajani, Saeed and Pouyafar, Vahid and Meshkabadi, Ramin and Volinsky, Alex A. and Bolouri, Amir",
    title = "Mechanical characterization of high volume fraction Al7075-Al\_2O\_3 composite fabricated by semisolid powder processing",
    year = "2023",
    journal = "The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology",
    volume = "125",

    issn = "0268-3768"
}


Abstract:
The mechanical properties and physical characteristics of aluminum alloy composites can be significantly improved by adding reinforcing phases. However, the high loading of the reinforcement phase in Al7075-Al_2O_3 composites has not been thoroughly studied. In this work, a combination of semisolid metal powder processing and powder metallurgy is used to process and manufacture Al7075-Al_2O_3 composites with a high reinforcement fraction of > 40 vol.%. The effects of processing parameters on the microstructures and mechanical properties of the composite material are discussed in detail. The loading limits of the high volume Al_2O_3 reinforcement in Al7075 composites are identified and linked to the processing parameters. A methodology is introduced to estimate the consolidation temperature of Al7075 alloy using compaction testing. Al_2O_3 particles (the average particle size of 120 µm) were mechanically milled with Al7075 powder (the average particle size of 20 µm) for 10 min and 5 h using a high-energy planetary ball mill. The mixture was then compacted in the semisolid state at 615 °C under the compaction pressures of 50 MPa and 100 MPa. By increasing the milling time from 10 min to 5 h, the deformation of aluminum powders and the fracture of Al_2O_3 reinforcement particles occur, restricting the loading limit of reinforcement. The milling time also shows a dominant effect on the powder morphology, microstructure, and mechanical properties of Al7075-Al_2O_3 composites. Increasing compaction pressure from 50 to 100 MPa significantly improved the compressive strength of the composite from 218 to 652 MPa. Al7075-Al_2O_3 composite with 40 vol.% of reinforcing phase exhibits the highest hardness of 198.2 HV and 96.9% relative density when it is milled for 5 h and compacted at 100 MPa. However, this composite shows the highest strength of 652 MPa when it is milled for 10 min. By increasing the reinforcing phase to 50 vol.% and 60 vol.%, the hardness, density, and compressive strength of composites decreased. The composites with 60 vol.% of reinforcing phase appeared overloaded. Results show that semisolid metal powder processing has huge potential for the fabrication of high loading Al_2O_3 in Al7075 matrix with near theoretical density.

Abstract:
In powder metallurgy (PM), severe plastic deformation (SPD) is a well-known technological solution to achieve interesting properties. However, the occurrence of pores in the final product may limit these properties. Also, for a given type of microstructure, the stereometric parameters of the pore structures, such as shape (represented by Aspect and Dcircle) and distribution (fshape, and fcircle), decisively affect the final properties. The influence of different processing routes (pressing, sintering and equal channel angular pressing (ECAP)) on pore structures in an aluminum PM alloy is discussed. The nature of porosity, porosity evolution and its behavior is explored. The correlation between pore size and morphology is also considered. The final pore structure parameters (Aspect, Dcircle, fshape, and fcircle) of studied aluminum alloys produced by different processing routes depends on the different formation routes.

Abstract:
In recent years, closed-cell porous Aluminum (Al) has drawn increasing attention, particularly in the applications requiring reduced weight and energy absorption capability such as in the automotive and aerospace industries. In the present work, porous Al with closed-cell structure was successfully fabricated by powder metallurgy technique using PMMA as a space holder. The effects of the amount of PMMA powder on the porosity, density, microstructure and compressive behaviors of the porous specimens were systematically evaluated. The results showed that closed-cell porous Al having different porosities (12%–32%) and densities (1.6478 g/cm3, 1.5125 g/cm3 and 1.305 g/cm3) could be produced by varying the amount of PMMA (20–30 wt %). Meanwhile, the compressive behavior results demonstrated that the plateau stress decreased and the energy absorption capacity increased with increasing amount of PMMA. However, the maximum energy absorption capacity was achieved in the closed-cell porous Al with the addition of 25 wt % PMMA. Therefore, fabrication of closed-cell porous Al using 25 wt % PMMA is considered as the optimal condition in the present study since the resultant closed-cell porous Al possessed good combinations of porosity, density and plateau stress, as well as energy absorption capacity.

Abstract:
Highly performance methods for cold pressing (cold die forging) of preforms from iron powder with subsequent heat treatment and producing ready parts made of powder are described in the paper. These methods allow fabricating parts with smooth surfaces and improved mechanical characteristics—porosity, tensile strength. Application of the traditional design set-up with a single-axial loading is restricted to high stresses in the dies to deform the preforms that lead to cracks formation. New powder compaction schemes by applying active friction forces (shear-enhanced compaction) make it possible to unload dies and produce high-quality parts by cold pressing. The scheme allows moving the die in the direction of the material flow with a velocity that exceeds the material flow velocity.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The Ni-Al system contains five intermetallic compounds, out of which NiAl and Ni3Al have received the vast majority of scientific and industrial interest over the past few decades. Ni3Al is of major interest due to its unique properties, including a yield strength that increases with temperature. The combustion synthesis (CS) process for producing Ni3Al from elemental powders of nickel and aluminum offers a low thermal budget and rapid processing, as well as purer products. This paper reviews the fundamentals of CS as applied to Ni3Al and its composites, and focuses on research over the past 25 years, including mechanically and electrically activated combustion synthesis and combined combustion synthesis and bulk deformation processes to produce high-density products. Several new directions are suggested for future research in the field.</jats:p>

The excerpt reports cold-isostatic pressing and sintering results for aluminum and iron powders. For soft aluminum, near-full densification was obtained at 400 MPa, while plastic deformation began above 100 MPa. The reported maximum sintered aluminum density was 99.3% at 600 MPa, followed by sintering at 600 °C for 20 minutes. The text states that aluminum density increased by only 1.5% during sintering, indicating that most densification occurred during pressing. For iron, plastic deformation began above 300 MPa; approximately 89% density was achieved at 600 MPa before sintering. The maximum reported sintered iron density was 91.5% at 600 MPa and 1200 °C for 30 minutes, although the body of the excerpt also reports a maximum of 90.3% at 1200 °C/30 minutes, suggesting a possible distinction or inconsistency between plotted and concluding values. Iron density increased by only 1.74% after sintering. SEM observations describe reduced porosity and complete plastic deformation at high pressure. The excerpt gives no numerical pore-size measurements, oxide analysis, green-strength values, or information about the Andasmas 2011 Al–Ni study; therefore oxide effects and direct comparison with that work cannot be established from this passage.

## pqac-00000016

From text 'kowalski1992somenewaspects pages 2-4'.

L. Kowalski, B. M. Korevaar, and J. Duszczyk. Some new aspects of the theory of oxidation and degassing of aluminium-based alloy powders. Journal of Materials Science, 27:2770-2780, Jan 1992. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00540704, doi:10.1007/bf00540704. This article has 52 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides useful baseline hydrogen and water-related information for gas-atomized aluminium alloy powders. Total hydrogen was reported as 24.5 ppm for air-atomized Al-Si-Cu-Mg powder and 19.8 ppm for nitrogen-atomized Al-Fe-Mo-Zr powder. Because these values greatly exceed hydrogen solubility in solid or molten aluminium (0.035 and 0.7 ppm, respectively), the authors infer that nearly all hydrogen is associated with the oxide layer, either as hydroxides or physically adsorbed water vapour, rather than dissolved hydrogen in the metal. Comparison with oxygen content, oxide thickness (approximately 5–7 nm), and powder surface area led them to conclude that the hydrogen quantity is sufficient to saturate the oxide’s outer layer with water. The excerpt also distinguishes atmospheric exposure: humid air can cause oxidation and bind water at the surface as hydrated alumina or physically adsorbed water. For degassing, compacted powder was heated under high vacuum at approximately 2.5 °C min−1 to above the hydrogen-evolution peak, while water and hydrogen were monitored by mass spectrometry. Samples were then exposed to normal atmosphere for 24 hours and degassed again. Exact evolved-water quantities, vacuum pressure, hold times, and complete desorption-temperature ranges are not given here; the air-atomized hydrogen curve is only shown to begin with a peak near 175 °C.

## pqac-00000017

From text 'estrada1991gasentrapmentand pages 6-8'.

J. L. Estrada, J. Duszczyk, and B. M. Korevaar. Gas entrapment and evolution in prealloyed aluminium powders. Journal of Materials Science, 26:1431-1442, Mar 1991. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00544650, doi:10.1007/bf00544650. This article has 38 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Estrada, Duszczyk, and Korevaar report hydrogen released from two air-atomized aluminium-alloy powders: powder J1 contained 24.58 ppm H, equivalent to 27.53 mL per 100 g, while K1 contained 13.09 ppm H, equivalent to 14.66 mL per 100 g. These values were measured at 550 °C and are stated to be 50–100 times higher than hydrogen levels in degassed cast alloys. The authors conclude that practically all measured hydrogen resides in the particle oxide layer as chemically or physically bound H2O, rather than as dissolved hydrogen in the aluminium matrix. The proposed degassing chemistry includes removal of adsorbed water vapour, dehydration of hydrated surface oxides/hydroxides (Al2O3·3H2O → Al2O3 + H2O), oxide formation involving oxygen, and reactions of aluminium or magnesium with water that produce molecular H2. Thus, the excerpt distinguishes adsorbed moisture and hydroxide/oxide-bound water conceptually, but does not provide separate numerical amounts for each fraction or a direct dissolved-H measurement. Vacuum degassing was tested from 20 to 550 °C at approximately 2.5 °C/min. Powder was cold-compacted at 160 MPa to about 65% theoretical density, leaving interconnected porosity. A turbomolecular-pump/quadrupole-mass-spectrometer system monitored released gases, but this excerpt gives no numerical vacuum pressure, dwell time, or discrete desorption-temperature ranges. It also contains no data from Kowalski 1992, Davis 1995, or Yamasaki 2004.

This excerpt from Davis, Miodownik, and Watts (1995) provides qualitative and temperature-resolved evidence for separating water species and hydrogen during degassing of gas-atomized aluminium-alloy powders, but it does not report absolute evolved quantities in mass percent, ppm, or mL per 100 g, nor does the excerpt specify vacuum pressure or degassing duration. It identifies an early desorption feature attributed to adsorbed water at approximately 100 °C. Chemically bonded or oxide/hydroxide-associated water is released at higher temperatures, with prior work cited as observing water evolution mainly between 120 and 200 °C. Hydrogen evolution occurs at substantially higher temperatures, typically about 350–450 °C, with a cited maximum near 400 °C; another cited result reports a water maximum near 200 °C. The text links hydrogen evolution to a rapid decline in the water signal, suggesting reaction of water-related surface species with alloy or surface components. The paper also reports greater hydrogen evolution for larger particle-size fractions and discusses carbonate decomposition with CO2 evolution. Complete degassing is described as requiring heating to the highest temperature compatible with avoiding structural degradation; prolonged treatment at lower temperature may be insufficient. Estrada (1991), Kowalski (1992), and Yamasaki (2004) are not covered in this excerpt, so their quantitative gas yields, pressures, and times cannot be extracted here.

## pqac-00000019

Estrada et al. (1991) distinguishes several gas-containing surface reservoirs in atomized aluminium powders. The particles have a hydrated oxide film containing both adsorbed water and hydroxide-bound water, described for aluminium as A1203·2Al(OH)3 and for magnesium-containing alloys as MgO–Mg(OH)2 mixtures, with physically adsorbed H2O/O2. The excerpt identifies progressive hydroxide/oxyhydroxide dehydration transformations over approximately 150–175 °C, 310–500 °C, and above 500 °C, but it does not provide numerical water or hydrogen yields in mass percent, ppm, or mL per 100 g. During heating, absorbed water is removed first; hydrogen can also arise from desorption of absorbed or dissolved hydrogen. At higher temperature, especially above about 400 °C, water reacts with oxide-free aluminium and magnesium, producing hydrogen through 2Al + 3H2O → Al2O3 + 3H2 and Mg + H2O → MgO + H2. Magnesium hydroxide and MgAl2O4 are noted as relatively stable and complicating degassing. Degassing effectiveness depends on equilibrium gas pressure, diffusion, surface reactions, temperature, and time; the cited relation gives concentration change as dependent on pressure and time and inversely on material thickness. No explicit vacuum pressure or degassing-time dataset is included in these pages.

This excerpt provides temperature and experimental-condition data relevant to quantifying water and hydrogen evolution from gas-atomized aluminum powder, but it does not report the evolved quantities in mass percent, ppm, or mL per 100 g. For temperature-programmed desorption, powders were heated at 5 K min−1 under 10−3 Pa vacuum, with desorbed gases analyzed continuously by quadrupole mass spectrometry. Powder exposure conditions included humid air (>40% moisture), dry air (<20 ppm moisture), and high-purity argon (<0.5 ppm oxygen and moisture), following 24-hour room-temperature exposure. Water desorption was measured separately, but numerical H2O amounts and desorption-temperature values are not included in the supplied pages. The excerpt distinguishes surface-adsorbed gases and water from chemically bound water in hydrated alumina/aluminum hydroxide. Hydrated-Al2O3 decomposition to crystalline Al2O3 occurred at 623 K, while hydrogen desorption occurred at approximately 620–660 K onset/increase and peaked at 725 K. Hydrogen was observed after humid-air exposure but not after dry-air or argon exposure, supporting a relationship to moisture-derived surface species. The proposed reactions separate oxide hydration conversion from subsequent hydrogen evolution: hydrated alumina reacts with aluminum to form crystalline alumina and surface hydrogen, followed by recombination of surface hydrogen into H2. XPS indicates conversion of amorphous trihydrated alumina to crystalline alumina around 623 K. Hydrogen evolution is attributed to reaction of aluminum with hydrated oxide, but the oxidation/decomposition and hydrogen-release steps are separated: hydrated oxide reacts around 623 K to produce chemisorbed surface hydrogen, while Hsurf recombines and desorbs as H2 around 725 K. The excerpt therefore helps distinguish adsorbed water, oxide-bound water, and chemisorbed hydrogen, while additional cited studies (Estrada 1991, Kowalski 1992, Davis 1995, and Yamasaki 2004) would be needed for quantitative loading, pressure, and time data.

H. Puga, J. Barbosa, D. Soares, F. Silva, and S. Ribeiro. Recycling of aluminium swarf by direct incorporation in aluminium melts. Journal of Materials Processing Technology, 209:5195-5203, Jun 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2009.03.007, doi:10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2009.03.007. This article has 136 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt provides direct evidence for remelting aluminium machining swarf formed into briquettes in an induction furnace, but it does not report aluminium powder, separate chip geometries, preheating, fluxed versus flux-free operation, stirring conditions, or post-remelting mechanical properties. The tested charge used ingot to form an initial molten pool, followed by swarf briquettes. The selected conditions were approximately 15 kg total charge, 33.3% initial ingot/molten pool and 66.7% swarf briquettes compacted at 300 bar, induction melting at 850 °C under argon for 60 minutes. At 300 bar, experiments produced about 88.2–91.3% metal incorporation, with 8.0–8.9% dross; at 400 bar, incorporation was 81.3–85.4% and dross 11.7–13.5%; at 500 bar, incorporation fell to 75.0–78.3% and dross rose to 14.6–18.8%. Higher compaction reduced briquette porosity, hindered molten-metal penetration, increased melting time, and apparently left metal in the dross. Argon increased average recovery from 60.8% to 83.3% and reduced oxidation and dross. Larger initial molten pools produced approximately 90% recovery, whereas pools near 20% yielded around 85% or lower. The excerpt mentions plunging compacted swarf but gives no quantified stirring or immersion/preheating comparison.

This excerpt provides direct evidence for remelting compacted aluminium machining swarf briquettes, including induction-furnace trials, but it does not report aluminium powder, loose chips, fluxed briquettes, or a direct powder-versus-chip comparison. Briquette density increased with compaction pressure from 2.03 kg/dm3 at 300 bar to 2.10 kg/dm3 at 500 bar, while moisture decreased from 2.83% to 2.42%. In induction melting with 33.3% briquettes, metal incorporation was 85.1% at 850 °C and 83.3% at 800 °C, with dross of 9.6% and 11.4% of briquette mass, respectively. Resistance-furnace results were poorer: 68.8% and 62.5% incorporation, with 27.1–32.3% dross. Argon protection improved recovery to 81.3–85.4%, compared with 58.7–62.0% without protection, and reduced dross from 32.5–34.8% to 11.7–13.5%. Between 800 and 950 °C, recovery was approximately 79.5–85.2% and dross 11.6–15.5%; above 850 °C, recovery and dross changed little, although melting time fell from 65 minutes at 800 °C to 50 minutes at 950 °C. The excerpt attributes induction effects to electromagnetic stirring, which can increase hydrogen pickup, oxidation, and transient element loss, but gives no quantitative immersion/preheating comparison, flux-use comparison, or final-property data.

This excerpt provides direct evidence for recycling aluminium machining swarf in induction melts, but not for aluminium powder or briquetted swarf specifically. It states that recycling performance depends on swarf conditioning, melting technique, and metal-treatment methodology. The identified critical measures are reducing chip moisture, induction melting under a protective atmosphere, and applying a specially developed degassing technique. The process reportedly achieved approximately 90% metal recovery with minimum dross formation and without traditional salts or fluxes. The excerpt does not provide quantitative comparisons of immersion versus preheating, melt time, melt temperature, stirring intensity, or charge-addition procedure. It also does not distinguish powder from chips, report briquette behavior, or compare fluxed and flux-free conditions beyond identifying the developed process as flux-free. The material-specific challenges are important: swarf has low bulk density (0.25 kg/dm3), an aluminium-oxide film, and machining-fluid contamination. Without suitable preparation, the text predicts low recovery, high energy use, smoke and gas generation, inclusions, porosity, and poor mechanical properties. In contrast, the developed treatment produced AlSi12Cu1 ingots with microstructure, soundness, and chemical composition similar to commercial second-melt material. Traditional recovery may lose up to 50% of the aluminium.

Abstract:
AA7075 aluminum alloy is widely used for several high-technology applications for its high mechanical strength to weight ratio but is still the subject of several studies seeking a further increase in its mechanical properties. A commercial powder is used, either as-received or after ball-milling. Dense AA7075 samples are prepared in one step by Spark Plasma Sintering, at 550 °C with a holding time of 15 min and a uniaxial pressure of 100 MPa. No additional heat treatment is performed. Laser granulometry, X-ray diffraction and optical- and scanning electron microscopy show that both grain size and morphology are preserved in the dense samples, due to the relatively low temperature and short sintering time used. The samples prepared using the ball-milled powder exhibit both higher Vickers microhardness and transverse fracture strength values than those prepared using the raw powder, reflecting the finer microstructure.

Abstract:
In this study, the nano-aluminum powder was reinforced with a hybrid of copper and graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs). The ratios of GNPs were 0 wt%, 0.4 wt%, 0.6 wt%, 1.2 wt% and 1.8 wt%. To avoid the reaction between aluminum and graphene and, consequently, the formation of aluminum carbide, the GNP was first metalized with 5 wt% Ag and then coated with the predetermined 15 wt% Cu by the electroless coating process. In addition, the coating process was performed to improve the poor wettability between metal and ceramic. The Al/(GNPs-Ag)Cu nanocomposites with a high relative density of 99.9% were successfully prepared by the powder hot-pressing techniques. The effects of (GNPs/Ag) and Cu on the microstructure, density, hardness, and compressive strength of the Al-Cu nanocomposite were studied. As a result of agitating the GNPs during the cleaning and silver and Cu-plating, a homogeneous distribution was achieved. Some layers formed nano-tubes. The Al4C3 phase was not detected due to coating GNPs with Cu. The Cu9Al4 intermetallic was formed during the sintering process. The homogeneous dispersion of Cu and different ratios of GNs, good adhesion, and the formation of the new Cu9Al4 intermetallic improved in hardness. The pure aluminum sample recorded 216.2 HV, whereas Al/Cu reinforced with 1.8 GNs recorded 328.42 HV with a 51.9% increment. The compressive stress of graphene samples was improved upon increasing the GNPs contents. The Al-Cu/1.8 GNs sample recorded 266.99 MPa.

Abstract:

                  <jats:p>Metal matrix composites find applications across various scientific disciplines and are in high demand worldwide. Consequently, it is imperative to enhance their mechanical properties promptly. The manufacturing of metal matrix composites poses challenges when utilizing conventional methods due to issues such as agglomeration, interfacial reactions, and wetting difficulties. Thus, the most efficient approach for producing metal matrix nano-composites (MMNCs) is through powder metallurgy in conjunction with cold iso-static compaction. This technique offers the advantage of eliminating defects like nano-particle clustering and ensuring a uniform distribution of reinforcement particles within the matrix. The primary aim of this study is to evaluate previous research regarding the capability of powder metallurgy to utilize a cold iso-static compaction chamber for achieving a consistent distribution within the metal matrix.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Hot isostatic pressing (HIP) technology can directly produce nearly clean shaped workpieces that meet the requirements while ensuring machining accuracy and surface quality. Usually, people use numerical simulation methods to reduce experimental costs. Generally, a uniform powder relative density distribution of about 65% is used in the simulation. However, in practical engineering, we found that even with additional tools such as vibration tables, the powder filling is not uniform. The non-uniform distribution causes uneven shrinkage of the powder and capsule after HIP. In this paper, a numerical model for HIPing of Ti-6Al-4V powder is developed to improve the prediction by comparing the uniform and non-uniform initial powder distribution. The results show that different initial relative density distributions affect the powder densification process and further affect the deformation of the capsule. It also leads to non-uniform stress distribution after HIP, which increases the risk of capsule rupture. The analysis of the numerical simulation results and the comparison with the experimental results highlights that taking into account the non-uniform powder distribution inside the capsule is vital to improve numerical results and produce near-net shape components. The maximum error of the simulation with the usual initial relative density setting of 65% is 4.2%. However, considering the uneven distribution of initial powder, the maximum error is reduced to 3.16%, and the average error is also less than 2%.

Abstract:
This work provides an overview of the aluminum (Al) recycling process, from the scrap upgrading to the melting process. Innovations and new trends regarding the Al recycling technologies are highlighted. Aluminum recycling offers advantages in terms of environmental and economic benefits. The presence of deleterious impurities in recycled Al alloys is increasing and this is the main drawback if compared to primary alloys. The continuous growth of undesired elements can be mitigated by different technologies, preliminary operations and treatments, and by the optimization of the melting process. Downgrading and dilution are possible solutions to reduce the rate of impurities, but they are not sustainable if the final use of Al alloy continuously increases. The main objectives in the development of the Al recycling are shown and discussed. In particular, the evolution of preliminary treatments of the scrap, as sorting, comminution and de-coating, is reported and a review of the melting technologies is also presented. However, the choice of performing preliminary operations to the melting stage, thus improving the operating conditions during the furnace running, is a trade-off between costs and process efficiency.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Recent studies revealed that the addition of different grain refiner master alloys can affect the sedimentation and thus the spatial distribution of double oxide films in the melt. In this work, the interactions of TiB
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    and (Al,Si)
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    Ti particles with bifilm defects were investigated in the case of a liquid Al-Si-Mg-Cu alloy. The interactions between refiner particles and bifilms were studied by optical and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), while the changes in melt quality were analyzed by the computed tomographic (CT) analysis of reduced pressure test (RPT) specimens. The sedimentation behavior of grain refiner particles was investigated through computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. It was found that TiB
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    particles tend to adhere to double oxide films suspended in the liquid metal, while (Al,Si)
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    Ti particles became attached to bifilms due to the heterogeneous nucleation of (Al,Si)
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    Ti on bifilms and the partial engulfment of oxide film segments during the growth of (Al,Si)
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    Ti particles. The attachment of grain refiner particles to double oxide films leads to the aided sedimentation of bifilms, which results in lowered porosity in RPT specimens. CFD simulations revealed that the experimentally observed fast sedimentation of TiB
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    can only be expected when relatively large particle agglomerates are created.
                  </jats:p>

La presence d'inclusions dans les alliages d'aluminium est l'un des problemes les plus serieux rencontres lors du moulage de ces alliages. Les inclusions reduisent les proprietes mecaniques et augmentent la porosite; elles sont nuisibles a la finition de la surface et elles ont tendance a augmenter la corrosion. Quelques inclusions non metalliques fragiles agissent en tant que concentrations de contraintes et peuvent causer des bris prematures des composantes. Avec la demande croissante de pieces coulees en aluminium de plus haute qualite, particulierement dans les industries de l'automobile et de l'aerospatiale, beaucoup d'attention a ete pretee a la proprete du metal liquide. 
 
L'amelioration de la proprete de la fonte d'aluminium peut etre effectuee par des techniques d'enlevement ou par la surveillance des inclusions. Du point de vue de controle ou de surveillance, un certain nombre de techniques, telles que PoDFA (Porous Disc Filtration Analysis), LAIS (Liquid Aluminum Inclusion Sampler), Prefil (Pressure Filtration), et Qualiflash ont ete developpees pour mesurer les inclusions dans les fontes d'aluminium. Cependant, ces techniques prennent du temps et peuvent seulement fournir des resultats en dehors de la ligne de coulee; par consequent, l'information est souvent obtenue trop tard pour faire les ajustements necessaires dans le processus de coulee. Actuellement, bien qu'il y ait une technique de mesure en ligne disponible, a savoir LiMCA II, celle-ci est trop chere et par consequent n'est generalement pas accessible. 
 
La technique de detection a ultrasons semble etre une methode prometteuse pour resoudre le probleme des inclusions en raison de sa capacite a sonder l'interieur des materiaux. La presente etude a ete entreprise pour etudier la capacite de la technique ultrasonique pour mesurer diverses inclusions dans l'aluminium et dans l'alliage commercial de type 356 a deux temperatures differentes. 
 
Des inclusions de T1B2, d'AlSr, d'A^Ti, et d'A^C^ ont ete ajoutees aux alliages d'aluminium utilises pour etre etudiees a l'aide d'une machine "Metalvision MV20/20 ultrasonic". Les donnees obtenues ont fourni des informations sur (i) la valeur de proprete de Faluminium, (ii) la dimension moyenne des particules, et (iii) le nombre total de particules pour chaque gamme de dimension particulaire, en fonction du temps d'essai. Un examen de la microstructure des echantillons solidifies obtenus a partir des prelevements de la fonte a ete egalement effectue en utilisant une microsonde electronique de type Jeol JXA-8900L. 
 
La comparaison entre les resultats obtenus par la technique ultrasonique et les mesures effectuees par microsonde sur les microstructures correspondantes a montre que la machine ultrasomque peut etre utilisee comme dispositif en ligne pour determiner la proprete de la fonte pendant une longue periode (5 h dans la presente etude). Les courbes de proprete du metal liquide obtenues par la machine ultrasonique sont fiables et peuvent etre employees comme guide pour les coulees a condition que la temperature du bain liquide et les conditions d'agitation soient correctement ajustees. 
 
L'augmentation de la concentration des inclusions reduit le niveau de proprete de la fonte et est refletee par une diminution correspondante de la courbe de proprete de la fonte illustree par la machine ultrasonique, indiquant ainsi sa reponse relative au changement du niveau d'inclusions. L'augmentation de la temperature de coulee du metal liquide accelere cependant la decomposition de l'alliage mere, augmentant le nombre de particules d'inclusions dans la fonte et reduisant de ce fait la valeur de proprete de fonte. 
 
Normalement, quand les inclusions TiB2 sont ajoutees a la fonte d'aluminium, la fluidite de la fonte diminue de maniere significative. Les autres techniques d'analyse des inclusions (LiMCA et toutes les autres techniques de filtration) peuvent seulement detecter les inclusions T1B2 quand leur concentration est tres basse (moins de 10 ppm). En appliquant la technique a ultrasons, des mesures peuvent etre conduites correctement pour des concentrations aussi hautes que 90 ppm. Ceci indique que la technique ultrasomque fournit une alternative amelioree pour la mesure des mclusions TIB2 dans raluminium liquide. Ce fait est d'importance, puisque les mclusions sont invariablement presentes en raison de l'addition de TIB2 qui est essentielle aux processus d'affinage de grain utilises pour raluminium.

## pqac-00000032

From text 'chua2014developmentofaluminum pages 52-57'.

AS Chua. Development of aluminum powder metallurgy alloys for aerospace applications. Unknown journal, 2014.

The excerpt compares PM2324 (an Al-2024-type powder metallurgy alloy) and PM7075 processed by die compaction versus cold isostatic pressing (CIP), but it does not provide a complete numerical green-density table at 100, 200, 300, and 400 MPa. For PM2324, only the approximate 100 MPa green-density range (81–84%) is stated; the figures indicate higher green density for CIP across the pressure range. Die-compacted PM2324 sintered density increased to about 300 MPa and then plateaued, whereas CIP sintered density was approximately pressure-independent. Tensile data show that CIP at 100 MPa produced 359 MPa yield strength and 412 MPa UTS, while die compaction required roughly 300 MPa for peak performance (367 MPa YS, 410 MPa UTS). The best PM2324 microstructures from both methods had high sinter quality, no visible prior-particle boundaries, and only sporadic, isolated, rounded porosity. For PM7075, green density also increased with pressure and CIP was higher than die pressing; at 100 MPa, densities were only about 72–74%. Low-pressure CIP PM7075 compacts were too fragile and irregular for dimensional or tensile testing, so complete CIP data begin at 200 MPa. The excerpt contains no quantitative die-wall-friction, lubricant, density-gradient, or pure-aluminum results.

## pqac-00000033

From text 'chua2014developmentofaluminum pages 47-52'.

AS Chua. Development of aluminum powder metallurgy alloys for aerospace applications. Unknown journal, 2014.

The excerpt directly compares die compaction and cold isostatic pressing (CIP) for PM2324, an aluminum powder-metallurgy alloy based on 2024. It does not provide tabulated exact green-density values at 100, 200, 300, and 400 MPa; the accompanying figure is not numerically reproduced in the text. It states that CIP produced higher green density across the tested pressure range, while both methods produced coherent, defect-free bodies and exceeded 90% theoretical density at pressures of at least 200 MPa. CIP’s advantage is attributed to isostatic loading and minimal die-wall friction, whereas uniaxial die pressing generated density gradients and more nonuniform length/width dimensional changes. For sintering, die-compacted PM2324 increased from 94.5% theoretical density at 100 MPa to 99.5% at pressures of 300 MPa and above. CIP samples reached 99.6 ± 0.1% theoretical density at all pressures, so the CIP benefit was strongest at low pressure and largely disappeared at 300–400 MPa. The blend contained 1.5 wt% wax lubricant removed during debinding. No specific porosity, tensile/handling-strength results, or comparable results for PM7075 or pure aluminum appear in this excerpt; therefore it should not be generalized to PURE Al.

## pqac-00000034

From text 'chua2014developmentofaluminum pages 43-47'.

AS Chua. Development of aluminum powder metallurgy alloys for aerospace applications. Unknown journal, 2014.

The excerpt describes a direct comparison of uniaxial die compaction and cold isostatic pressing (CIP) for the aluminum PM alloys PM2324 and PM7075, which are based on wrought 2024 and 7075 compositions. Both methods used compaction pressures of 100, 200, 300, and 400 MPa. Die compaction used floating-die rigid tooling and produced TRS and Charpy bars, while CIP used evacuated rubber molds and produced cylindrical compacts. Green density was measured by the Archimedes method according to MPIF Standard 42. The study reports that comparable sintered product quality could be obtained by either method. ## pqac-00000040

From text 'sweet2014advancedsinteringtechniquesa pages 55-61'.

G Sweet. Advanced sintering techniques of aluminum: spark plasma sintering. Unknown journal, 2014.

The excerpt provides SPS data for pure Al and Al–0.4Mg powder, rather than conventional vacuum hot pressing or a direct argon-versus-vacuum comparison. Under 50 MPa applied pressure and a heating rate of 100 K min−1, density increased with sintering temperature, with pure Al requiring approximately 600°C for full densification and reaching up to 99.97% relative density. A 0.4% Mg addition disrupted the particle-surface oxide and enabled full densification at roughly 100°C lower temperature. Hold time and heating rate produced comparatively minor property gains, while applied pressure and temperature were the dominant variables. Increased thermal exposure caused microstructural coarsening and reduced hardness; oxide-rich prior-particle boundaries remained visible even after sintering at 600°C. SPS also reduced surface-derived gases and impurities. Hydrogen removal was strongest at 600°C, leaving approximately 5–10 ppm, comparable to wrought aluminum alloys. Oxygen decreased substantially but remained detectable, with magnesium influencing the final oxygen level. The text attributes gas removal partly to decomposition of hydrated oxide films and notes that conventional vacuum degassing normally requires hours, moderate temperature, low pressure, and interconnected porosity for evacuation. No direct data are given here for 300–550°C vacuum hot pressing, 500–640°C argon versus vacuum sintering, pressure/dwell schedules beyond 50 MPa, or limitations relative to cold compaction for subsequent melting.

The excerpt supports the assessment that aluminum dust presents a severe combustible-dust explosion hazard. It states that aluminum is among the most explosive metal dusts and identifies the deflagration index KST as a quantitative measure based on the maximum pressure-rise rate and vessel volume: KST = (dP/dt)max V1/3. Higher KST values correspond to more severe explosions, and pure aluminum is identified as a high-KST Class ST-328 dust. The text cautions that explosivity depends substantially on particle size and shape, airborne concentration, and surface oxidation, which is relevant to evaluating a 15–63 micron fraction. It also describes electrostatic discharge as a plausible ignition source and recommends nitrogen purging/inerting to prevent flammable atmospheres in process equipment. For dryers, automated pressure-based interlocks, alarms, rotation shutdown, and nitrogen purge are suggested. The excerpt does not provide specific minimum ignition energy (MIE), minimum explosible concentration (MEC), or KST values specifically for 15–63 micron aluminum dust. It also does not address vacuum-pump-line filtration, metal-fire water-response procedures, personnel safety, or CIP pressure-vessel hazards in detail. Those topics require additional authoritative sources such as NFPA, OSHA, CSB, manufacturer data, and validated explosibility testing.

Aluminum is classified among the extremely reactive metal dusts and can correspond to the most severe St3 hazard class. The article reports aluminum values above 300 bar·m/s for KSt, above 10 bar for Pmax, and below 10 mJ for minimum ignition energy; its tabulated representative values are KSt 515 bar·m/s and Pmax 11.2 bar. In a comparison of test vessels, aluminum KSt increased from 162 bar·m/s in a 20-L sphere to 328 bar·m/s in a 1-m³ chamber, demonstrating that standardized small-vessel testing may underestimate severity. The authors attribute this scale effect partly to thermal radiation, which can be much stronger for metal dusts than for organic dusts. The excerpt also warns that highly reactive metal powders may burn in carbon dioxide, water vapor, and nitrogen, so inerting assumptions require validation for the specific aluminum powder and process. It identifies aluminum’s ignition sensitivity, pyrophoric potential of ultrafine particles, and high-temperature combustion as important safety considerations.

This excerpt provides published experimental information specifically for wet-bag cold isostatic pressing of pure iron powder, not a direct wet-bag versus dry-bag comparison. The apparatus was a wet-type CIP press using a thin-wall natural-rubber mold (1 mm thick) contained in a perforated aluminum fixture; the fixture was sealed with covers, bolts, and nuts for waterproofing, and air was evacuated from the mold before pressing. The mold was 40 mm high and 40 mm in diameter, while the alloy-steel mandrel was 40 mm high and 20 mm in diameter. Iron powder ASC 100.29, with an average particle size of 80 μm, was compacted around the mandrel to tap density. Smooth and coarse mandrels (reported roughness 0.8 S and 25 S) were used to study tooling friction. The paper’s central finding or subject is that powder–mandrel friction disturbs powder flow and produces density inhomogeneity, despite CIP’s usual advantage of homogeneous, isotropic microstructure. Mandrel friction coefficients were inferred from the relationship between compaction pressure and mandrel ejection pressure, and finite-element simulations using the Shima–Oyane constitutive model were compared with experiments. Abstract:
Al:Zr, Al-8Mg:Zr, and Al-38Mg:Zr nanocomposite particles fabricated by physical vapor deposition (PVD) and ball milling were reacted in 1 atm of pure O2 within a custom, highly-sensitive micro-bomb calorimeter. The heats of combustion were compared to examine the effect of particle size and composition on combustion efficiency under room temperature and in a fixed volume. All particles yielded ~60–70% of their theoretical maximum heat of combustion and exhibited an increase in heat over composite thin films of similar compositions, which is attributed to an increase in the surface area to volume ratio. The effect of particle size and geometry are mitigated owing to the sintering of the particles within the crucible, implying the importance of particle dispersion for enhanced performance. Vaporization of the metal species may transition between two diffusion flame species (Mg to Al). As Mg content is increased, more vaporization may occur at lower temperatures, leading to an additional stage of sintering. Physically intermixed Al and Mg oxides have been observed coating the surface of the particles, which implies a continuous transition of these vaporization processes. Such nano-oxides imply high vapor-flame combustion temperatures (>2700 K) and suggest viability for agent defeat applications.

Abstract:
The connective hard tissues bone and teeth are highly porous on a micrometer scale, but show high values of compression strength at a relatively low weight. The fabrication of porous materials has been actively researched and different processes have been developed that vary in preparation complexity and also in the type of porous material that they produce. Methodologies are available for determination of pore properties. The purpose of the paper is to give an overview of these methods, the role of porosity in natural porous materials and the effect of pore properties on the living tissues. The minimum pore size required to allow the ingrowth of mineralized tissue seems to be in the order of 50 µm: larger pore sizes seem to improve speed and depth of penetration of mineralized tissues into the biomaterial, but on the other hand impair the mechanical properties. The optimal pore size is therefore dependent on the application and the used material.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    In this work, Porous copper foam samples were fabricated by a space-holder technique with water-atomized copper powder and sodium chloride (NaCl) particles in weight fractions ranging from 10 to 35 wt%. The powders were mechanically mixed at a 10:1 ball-to-powder ratio and 150 rpm for 2 h. The effects of space-holder content on the physical, mechanical, tribological, and electrochemical performance were systematically investigated. Increasing the NaCl fraction precisely controlled the total porosity, from 39.15% to 57.76%, and reduced the bulk density from 5.452 to 3.785 g/cm³. XRD and SEM analyses confirmed a single-phase FCC copper matrix and a structural transition from isolated pores to a highly interconnected open-cell network. Consequently, Vickers hardness, compressive yield strength, energy absorption capacity decreased from 52.12 to 29.23 HV, 18.25 to 1.65 MPa, and 35.73 to 10.46 MJ/m³, respectively, following a modified Gibson–Ashby model (R
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                     = 0.95). Concurrently, the coefficient of friction and specific wear rate increased (reaching a maximum of 0.73 mm³/N·m under 15 N for 35 wt% NaCl) due to strut thinning and localized delamination. Electrochemical evaluation in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution revealed an optimization threshold for sample fabricated with 25 wt% NaCl, which exhibited the lowest corrosion rate of 0.918 mm/y, and the highest polarization resistance (Rp) of 267.28 Ω, due to a stable Cu
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O passive film. Exceeding this threshold at 30 and 35 wt% NaCl led to structural instability and stagnant electrolyte zones, accelerating corrosion kinetics. Overall, lower-porosity porous copper foam architectures offer superior structural energy absorption, whereas the 25 wt% NaCl configuration achieves an optimal balance between mechanical integrity and corrosion resistance.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
The cover systems in contaminated sites have some problems, including desiccation cracks, which would lead to degradation of the barrier performance. This study presented a systemic laboratory experimental investigation on the liquid–plastic limit, moisture retention, hydraulic conductivity (k), and gas diffusion barrier properties of amended compacted clay by attapulgite and diatomite for controlling desiccation cracks and migration of water and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). The results showed that the attapulgite could enhance the moisture retention and liquid limit of amended compacted clay. Diatomite could reduce the gas diffusion coefficient (Dθ) significantly. The compacted clay amended by the dual-additives component of attapulgite and diatomite could enhance the liquid limit, moisture retention percent, gas barrier property, and hydraulic performance compared with the unamended clay. Based on the experimental data obtained, the dosage of additives was targeted to be 5%. The moisture retention percent of dual-additives (attapulgite 4% and diatomite 1%) amended clay increased by 82%, the k decreased by 25%, and the Dθ decreased by 42% compared with unamended clay. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM), BET-specific surface area test method (BET), Mercury Intrusion Porosimetry (MIP), and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) indicated the enhancement mechanism of additives-amended compacted clay.

Four Ti–Al compositions were examined, corresponding to Al3Ti, AlTi, AlTi + AlTi3, and AlTi3, so the reported behavior includes both near-stoichiometric intermetallic compositions and a two-phase composition. For Ti–40 wt% Al (TiAl), two exothermic events occurred. The first ignited at approximately 550 °C, with the broader first-peak ignition range reported as 520–570 °C; this ignition temperature was essentially insensitive to heating rate. The second event is associated with aluminium melting and liquid Al reacting with solid Ti: at heating rates of 10 K min−1 or less, ignition occurs near aluminium’s melting point (about 660 °C). At higher heating rate, ignition shifts lower; at 50 K min−1 it begins below the Al melting point, indicating a possible solid Al–solid Ti reaction contribution. Thus, the approximately 500–570 °C ignition applies to the first Ti–Al exotherm, while the second ignition is near 660 °C at low heating rate and can fall below 660 °C at high heating rate. The excerpt provides useful process data for remelting aluminium swarf briquettes, although it does not directly address mixtures of Al powder with Si, Cu, Mg, Mn, Fe, Ni, Ti, or Zr, nor does it report pure-powder solubility limits or intermetallic formation. In an induction furnace, an argon atmosphere increased average aluminium recovery from 60.8% to 83.3% by reducing oxidation and dross generation. Briquette density strongly affected melting: lower compaction pressure produced higher recovery, while increased pressure reduced porosity, hindered molten-metal penetration, lengthened melting time, and increased dross. Briquettes compacted at 300 bar performed better than those compacted at 400–500 bar; the reported 300-bar trials produced approximately 88.2–91.3% recovery, compared with roughly 75.0–78.3% at 500 bar. Initial molten-pool size also mattered: pools above 33.3% of the charge achieved approximately 90% recovery, whereas around 20% reduced recovery to about 85% or lower, likely because briquettes contacted the atmosphere and oxidized. The selected conditions were approximately 15 kg charge, 33.3% initial molten pool, 66.7% briquettes, 300-bar compaction, 850 °C, argon, and 60 minutes.
